guides.title: Best Beaches and Pools in Madeira: 14 Places to Swim
guides.summary: Madeira is mostly rock and pebble, so swimming means lava pools, lidos and a few sand beaches. Fourteen bathing places compared, with entry fees and opening details as of November 2026.
guides.html:
If you picture long sandy beaches, Madeira will surprise you. The island rises steeply from the sea, and most of its shore is cliff, boulders and dark pebbles. Swimming here usually means a lava rock pool filled by the Atlantic, a bathing complex with sea-water pools and a ladder into the sea, or one of a handful of beaches, two of them built with imported sand. The long sandy beach of the archipelago is on Porto Santo, a ferry ride away.

Below are the fourteen bathing places we cover, grouped by kind. Fees and opening hours are as published by the operators and checked in November 2026; they change, so check again before you go. All of them are on our beaches page, which you can filter by region.

Before you swim: what to expect

  • The sea is the open Atlantic. Swell arrives with little warning, especially on the north coast and in winter. Swim where there are lifeguards, use ladders and pool entries rather than rocks, and stay out when waves are breaking over the pool walls.
  • Lifeguards are seasonal in many places. Several beaches below are watched only during the bathing season; a few complexes are supervised all year.
  • Pebbles are hard on bare feet. Water shoes make entering and leaving the sea at pebble beaches much easier.
  • Water temperature stays mild all year but is not tropical. See the weather page for monthly figures, and the best time to visit for the swimming season.
  • In an emergency at sea, call 112 (see emergency contacts).

Sand beaches

Madeira has only a few sand beaches, and they are a mix of imported golden sand and natural dark volcanic sand.

Calheta beach (imported sand, west coast)

Calheta beach was Madeira's first artificial beach. Visit Madeira says it opened in 2004 with golden sand imported from Morocco, is about 100 metres long and is protected by two breakwaters, which help shelter the water. Access is free, and there are sun loungers and parasols, a bar, changing rooms and first aid. Check sea conditions and lifeguard cover before swimming with small children. It sits in the village of Calheta.

Machico beach (imported sand, east coast)

Machico has golden sand imported from Morocco in its sheltered bay, close to the airport. Visit Madeira's listing for the sandy Banda d'Além stretch mentions changing cabins, showers, toilets and parking, and a lifeguard during the bathing season. The town of Machico is right behind it, so this is an easy first or last swim of a trip.

Prainha do Caniçal (natural dark sand, east coast)

Prainha near Caniçal is one of the few natural sand beaches on Madeira: Visit Madeira describes its sand as volcanic and coppery, in an arid landscape near Ponta de São Lourenço. It has a restaurant, changing rooms and toilets, parasols, sun loungers and parking. Combine it with the coastal walk out to the headland or the Whale Museum in Caniçal.

Seixal beach (natural black sand, north coast)

Seixal beach is a small black sand beach that formed naturally a few years ago next to the harbour and the Clube Naval do Seixal, under the green cliffs of the north coast. There are showers, a bar and kayak hire; the Porto Moniz council lists free showers and toilets. Check the sea conditions before entering the water on this Atlantic coast. Seixal is part of the Porto Moniz and Seixal area.

Pebble beaches

Praia Formosa (Funchal)

Praia Formosa, west of the centre of Funchal, is what Visit Madeira calls the largest public beach in Madeira: four beaches together, over 2 km long, of pebbles and black sand. Access is free, lifeguards cover the bathing season, and there is parking, changing rooms, a first-aid post and a playground. A seafront promenade runs along it towards the Lido. Lifeguards are seasonal, so outside the bathing season it is better for a walk than a swim when the sea is lively.

Praia do Garajau (Caniço)

Garajau beach lies below the cliffs at Garajau, east of Funchal, inside the Garajau marine reserve, and its clear water is popular for snorkelling and diving. You can walk down or take the Garajau cable car, which Visit Madeira says opened in 2007 and runs from 10:00 to 18:00 in winter and to 20:00 in summer, as of November 2026. There is a snack bar, a diving centre, toilets, changing rooms and first aid. It is close to Caniço.

Fajã dos Padres (Ribeira Brava)

Fajã dos Padres is a strip of vineyards, vegetable plots and pebble beach at the foot of a high cliff on the south coast, between Câmara de Lobos and Ribeira Brava. The usual way down is the cable car, which takes about four minutes; as of November 2026, the operator lists 10:00 to 20:30 from 27 June to 13 September and 10:00 to 18:00 during the rest of the year. The fare is not published on the tourism board's page, so check it before you go. Below there is a small restaurant. Plan your return around the cable-car operating hours. Ribeira Brava is the next town to the west.

Ponta do Sol beach (west coast)

Ponta do Sol beach is a small pebble beach of about 160 metres between the cliffs of the valley, in front of the village of Ponta do Sol. It has changing rooms and toilets adapted for reduced mobility, a bar and parking nearby. The village's seafront and pier are a short walk away.

Lava rock pools

Pools formed or shaped from volcanic rock and refilled by the sea are Madeira's signature swimming places. Most have a wall or natural barrier against the swell, but waves can still break in on rough days.

Porto Moniz natural pools (north-west tip)

The Porto Moniz natural pools are the best known on the island. The municipality says entry is charged all year: €3 for adults and anyone over 3, free for children aged 3 and under, as of November 2026. They are open all year, from 9:00 to 17:00 in winter and to 19:00 in summer, with lifeguards on duty, a bar, changing rooms, a playground, first aid and loungers and parasols for hire. Nearby, at the entrance to the village, the free Cachalote pools are supervised in the bathing season but have only an outdoor shower. Read more about Porto Moniz, and pair the swim with the Achadas da Cruz cable car along the same coast.

Seixal natural pools (north coast)

Seixal has two sets of rock pools, both on our Seixal natural pools page. Poças das Lesmas, near Laje beach, have had lifeguards since 2024; Visit Madeira gives the entry fee as €2.50 as of November 2026 and lists toilets, showers and a bar, and warns that large waves can arise suddenly. The Clube Naval do Seixal pools by the harbour are free between 10:00 and 19:00 as of November 2026, according to the municipality, with a bar, showers and toilets.

Doca do Cavacas (Funchal)

Doca do Cavacas is a small complex of natural pools of volcanic origin with direct access to the sea, between the Lido and Praia Formosa, looking west to Cabo Girão. It is run by Frente MarFunchal, the city's bathing-complex company, at the same 2026 prices as the Lido (below), and, as of November 2026, opens every day from 10:00 to 18:00 in its listed hours for 25 October to 31 March. There are showers, toilets, changing rooms, a snack bar and loungers for hire.

Bathing complexes

Complexo Balnear do Lido (Funchal)

The Lido bathing complex is Funchal's best-known bathing place, with almost a century of history according to Visit Madeira. It has sea-water pools for adults and children, direct access to the sea, and lifts, ramps and amphibious chairs for visitors with reduced mobility. It is open all year and supervised. As of November 2026, Frente MarFunchal's 2026 price list gives a daily entry of €6.00 for adults, €2.00 for young people aged 7 to 17 and for retirees with Portuguese pension proof, and free entry for children up to 6 with an adult; its listed hours for 25 October to 31 March are 09:00 to 18:00. The Lido is the easy answer for a winter swim in the city, and the Lido promenade continues west to Doca do Cavacas and Praia Formosa.

The same company runs the Ponta Gorda and Barreirinha complexes; Barreirinha overlooks the harbour beside the old town.

Porto Santo

Porto Santo beach

Porto Santo beach is the archipelago's long sandy beach: Visit Madeira describes it as stretching for 9 km along the whole south coast of the island, with warm, clear water and calm areas on most days, though swell near the shore can make entry harder at times. Reach it on the Lobo Marinho ferry or a short flight; our Porto Santo travel guide and the day trip page cover fares and timetables.

Ponta da Calheta (Porto Santo)

Ponta da Calheta is the south-west end of the same beach, quieter and rockier, facing the islet Ilhéu da Cal (Ilhéu de Baixo). It has parking, changing rooms, toilets and a restaurant, and it is a good place for sunset.

Swimming in winter

Madeira is a year-round destination, but swimming in winter takes more planning. The Funchal complexes and the Porto Moniz pools are open all year with published winter hours, and offer supervised swimming when conditions permit. Lifeguard cover is seasonal at several natural beaches. Winter storms can make swimming and coastal access unsafe: respect closure signs and stay out when conditions are dangerous. Our Madeira in winter guide covers the season in full.

Which to choose

  • With small children: Calheta or Machico for sand and calm water; the Lido for pools with supervision.
  • For snorkelling: Garajau, inside the marine reserve.
  • For the classic lava pools: Porto Moniz, and Seixal on the same trip.
  • Staying in Funchal without a car: the Lido, Doca do Cavacas and Praia Formosa, linked by the seafront.
  • For a long sandy beach: Porto Santo.

Other ways to enjoy the sea include whale and dolphin watching, scuba diving and surfing. For where to base yourself near the beaches, see where to stay in Madeira.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Madeira have sandy beaches?

A few. Calheta and Machico have imported golden sand, and Prainha near Caniçal and Seixal have natural dark volcanic sand. Most of Madeira's coast is pebble and rock, and the long sandy beach of the archipelago is on Porto Santo.

How much does it cost to swim at the Porto Moniz natural pools?

As of November 2026, the municipality charges €3 per entry for adults and anyone over 3, with children aged 3 and under free. The nearby Cachalote pools are free but have almost no facilities.

How much is entry to the Lido in Funchal?

As of November 2026, Frente MarFunchal's 2026 price list gives €6.00 for an adult daily entry, €2.00 for ages 7 to 17 and eligible retirees, and free entry for children up to 6 with an adult. The same prices apply at Doca do Cavacas.

Can you swim in Madeira in winter?

Yes, but choose places with year-round supervision, such as the Funchal bathing complexes and the Porto Moniz pools. Lifeguard cover at many natural beaches is seasonal, and winter swells can be dangerous.

Which Madeira beach is best for snorkelling?

Garajau beach, east of Funchal, is inside the Garajau marine reserve, and its clear water and diving centre make it a good choice for snorkelling on the south coast.
guides.bestTime: June to October for swimming; the Funchal complexes and Porto Moniz pools open all year
guides.duration: Half a day per beach or pool
guides.budget: Most beaches are free; pools and complexes charge a modest entry fee, from €2.50 to €6.00 per adult as of November 2026

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Madeira: Month-by-Month Guide
guides.summary: Madeira works all year. Funchal's mean daily high stays between 19.9C and 26.8C, the sea at Funchal averages 18 to 23.5C, and the real choice is between dry summer weather, the April to June festivals and quieter, wetter winter walking.
guides.html:
The short version

Madeira has no bad month, only different trade-offs. On the south coast around Funchal, the official 1991 to 2020 normals from IPMA, Portugal's weather and climate institute, give a mean daily high of 20.0C in January and 26.8C in August. The gap between the warmest and coolest months is under seven degrees. What changes far more through the year is rain, wind on the north coast, conditions on the high trails and the number of people in town.

For most visitors the strongest months are April to June and September. April to June brings the Flower Festival and the Atlantic Festival fireworks, long days and a drying climate. September keeps the warmest sea of the year, averaging 23.5C at Funchal, before the autumn rains return in October. Winter suits walkers and winter-sun visitors who accept more rain; our Madeira in winter guide covers December to February in detail.

Three climates on one island: south, north and the peaks

Madeira's mountains split the weather. The official tourism board puts it simply: the south is usually warmer and drier. The north coast around Santana, São Vicente and Porto Moniz catches more cloud and rain from the prevailing winds. Above roughly the cloud line, around Pico do Arieiro and Pico Ruivo, it can be cold, wet and windy while Funchal sits in sunshine.

Every figure below names its station. They are long-run averages from IPMA, not forecasts:

  • Funchal Observatory (station 522, 58 m): full 1991 to 2020 monthly normals.
  • Porto Santo (station 524, 78 m): full 1991 to 2020 monthly normals.
  • Santana (north coast) and Chão do Areeiro (the uplands, below the summit of Pico do Arieiro): January and September 1991 to 2020 normals only, worked out from IPMA's monthly bulletins as observation minus anomaly. A complete twelve-month table for these two stations was not found.
  • The airport at Santa Catarina: we could not retrieve a station-specific 1991 to 2020 sheet, so no table is given here.

Highs and lows are IPMA mean daily maximum and minimum temperatures, 1991 to 2020. Rain days are days with at least 1 mm. Sea temperatures are our averages of the monthly means measured at Funchal from 1991 to 2020, in the IPMA series published by the regional statistics office (DREM). They describe the water off Funchal, not every bathing place, and not Porto Santo.

Two patterns stand out. Funchal's wettest months are October to December, each with more than 80 mm on average, while June to August are almost dry. And the Porto Santo station, at 78 m, is a little cooler by day than Funchal but much drier over the year: 381.7 mm against 574.3 mm.

The north coast and the mountains

The numbers for Santana show why a north-coast day needs its own plan. In January its normal high is 16.1C with 106.9 mm of rain, against 20.0C and 67.1 mm in Funchal. In September Santana's normal high is 22.8C. The uplands are another climate again: at Chão do Areeiro the January normal is a high of 8.7C and a low of 2.8C, with 225.4 mm of rain, more than three times Funchal's total. In September the same station's normal high is 16.7C. IPMA's January 2026 bulletin notes precipitation that fell at times as snow on the high ground.

The practical rule: pack a warm, waterproof layer for any trip above the cloud line, even in August, and choose the coast you base yourself on with the season in mind. Our where to stay guide compares the regions, and the Madeira weather page has the full station notes.

Season by season

January to March: green, quiet and changeable

Winter brings cool sea temperatures (18.0 to 18.9C at Funchal), but daytime highs near 20C on the south coast. The laurel forest of the Laurisilva is a rewarding option, subject to weather and access conditions. Walking is good on dry days, but storms can close classified trails and snow can close the road to Pico do Arieiro. The Madeira Carnival runs in downtown Funchal from 3 to 14 February 2027, with the allegorical parade on 5 and 6 February.

April to June: flowers, fireworks and the best walking light

Rain falls away quickly in spring: Funchal averages 45.2 mm in April and only 7.8 mm in June. Consider this walking window, with longer days, flowering gardens such as the Madeira Botanical Garden and Monte Palace Tropical Garden, with weather checks still essential for mountain trips. The Madeira Island Ultra Trail takes over the island's trails on 24 and 25 April 2027. The Flower Festival runs from 29 April to 30 May 2027, with the Great Allegoric Flower Parade listed for 2 and 16 May. The Atlantic Festival fills June: entertainment in Funchal from 4 to 27 June 2027 and the international fireworks contest on the Saturdays of 5, 12, 19 and 26 June.

July and August: dry, warm and busiest

High summer is the driest time in Funchal (1.3 to 1.7 mm of rain a month) and the sea climbs past 22C. It is the best time for swimming at the Porto Moniz natural pools or the Lido bathing complex, and for a Porto Santo day trip to the long sand of Porto Santo beach. The Feast of Our Lady of Monte peaks on 14 and 15 August, and the Madeira Wine Festival runs from 22 August to 12 September 2027. Book transport and accommodation ahead for summer trips.

September and October: warm sea, harvest and the first rains

September is quietly one of the best months: the sea averages 23.5C at Funchal, rain is still light (23.1 mm), and the wine harvest is under way. Porto Santo celebrates the Columbus Festival from 23 to 26 September 2027. October is still warm, with a 25.2C mean high, but it is the month the rain returns, averaging 91.2 mm in Funchal. The Madeira Nature Festival, from 5 to 10 October 2027, is built around walking, canyoning and time on the water.

November and December: wet weeks and the festive season

November and December are wet months in Funchal, but the sea is still above 20C and the city fills for the holidays. The Christmas lights are scheduled from 1 December 2026 to 10 January 2027, with the Market Night at the Mercado dos Lavradores on 23 December, and the year ends with the New Year fireworks over the bay. See our New Year fireworks guide for planning that night.

Levada and hiking season

You can walk in Madeira all year, but the best conditions for the classic routes, the Pico do Arieiro to Pico Ruivo hike (PR1), Levada das 25 Fontes (PR6) and Levada do Caldeirão Verde (PR9), come in the drier months from late spring to early autumn. Winter brings mud, falling rocks and more frequent closures.

Whatever the month, three rules apply as of November 2026. Independent non-resident visitors pay a fee for classified trails managed by IFCN and covered by its booking regime: 4.50 euros for an individual trail, 10.50 euros for the full PR1 to Pico Ruivo, when that route is open. Children aged 12 and under are exempt; residents of Madeira and visitors with a documented disability of at least 60%, with one accompanying legal guardian, also qualify for exemptions. Visitors must reserve each covered trail in advance on the regional SIMplifica portal and pay online unless exempt. Fee-exempt visitors still need a booking. There is no booking or fee payment at IFCN offices. And trail status changes often: IFCN, the regional forests and nature institute, opens and closes routes after storms, fires and repair works, and the IFCN status table read on 16 November 2026, updated on 13 November, marks PR1 closed, while PR6 and PR9 are open. Do not treat the older PR1 weekday restriction in the FAQ as permission to walk a closed route. Check the official IFCN trail-status page on the morning you walk. Our trail fees guide and levada walks guide go into the details, and the levada walks page lists the main routes.

Sea and swimming

The sea never gets truly cold or truly warm. At Funchal the monthly average ranges from 18.0C in March to 23.5C in September. Most swimmers will find June to October most comfortable, with the water at 20.7C or more. August and September have the highest monthly sea-temperature averages in this series. For whale and dolphin watching and scuba diving, a calm sea matters more than the month: check the marine forecast and your operator's call on the day.

Crowds and prices

Compare room rates and hire-car availability for your dates, especially around the festivals and public holidays. Book ahead if your plans depend on a particular hotel or vehicle. For calendar planning, our 2027 public holidays guide lists every date.

Practical notes

Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal and keeps the same clock time as mainland Portugal and the UK: UTC in winter and UTC+1 in summer. Getting between the coasts takes longer than the map suggests, so read our getting around guide before you choose a base. Whenever you come, pack a waterproof and a warm layer for the mountains, and leave room in the plan for a weather day spent at a wine lodge or on a Madeira wine tasting.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best month to visit Madeira?

For most people, May, June or September. May and June have dry, settled weather on the south coast, long days and the Flower and Atlantic festivals. September has the warmest sea of the year at Funchal (23.5C on average) and light rain before October's wetter weather.

Is Madeira warm in winter?

Mild rather than hot. Funchal's mean daily high is 20.0C in January and 19.9C in February, with lows around 14C. The north coast and the mountains are much cooler: the January normal high at Chão do Areeiro, in the uplands, is 8.7C.

When is the rainy season in Madeira?

Most rain falls from October to March. In Funchal, October, November and December each average more than 80 mm, while July and August average under 2 mm. The north coast and the mountains can be much wetter than Funchal.

When is the sea warmest in Madeira?

August and September. The Funchal series averages 23.3C in August and 23.5C in September, and 22.7C in October. The coolest water is in February and March, at about 18C.

When is the best time for levada walks?

Late spring to early autumn gives the driest, most reliable conditions, especially April to June and September. You can walk in winter, but closures after storms are more frequent. In any month, book each classified trail on Simplifica and check IFCN's trail-status page on the day.

Can it snow in Madeira?

Yes, on the highest ground. IPMA reported precipitation falling at times as snow in January 2026, and the regional roads authority has closed the ER 202 road between Poiso and Pico do Arieiro because of snow. Snow is a high-ground hazard rather than a reason to expect a snowy coastal holiday.

Is Porto Santo's weather different from Madeira's?

Yes. Porto Santo is much drier: 381.7 mm of rain a year at its station against 574.3 mm in Funchal. Its mean highs run slightly below Funchal's, from 18.2C in February to 25.7C in August.

When are the main festivals in 2027?

Carnival from 3 to 14 February, the Flower Festival from 29 April to 30 May, the Atlantic Festival from 4 to 27 June, the Wine Festival from 22 August to 12 September and the Columbus Festival on Porto Santo from 23 to 26 September. The official calendar is subject to updates, so check the events page closer to your trip.

guides.title: Getting Around Madeira: Buses, Aerobus, Car Hire, Ferry
guides.summary: Madeira's SIGA buses cost from €1.45 a trip on a GIRO card, the Aerobus links the airport and Funchal, and the Lobo Marinho ferry takes about 2h15 to Porto Santo. Fares as of November 2026.
guides.html:
Madeira is small on the map and slow on the ground. Roads climb steeply from the coast into the mountains, the island is threaded with tunnels, and the north coast feels far from Funchal even when the distance is short. A city break works well on foot and by bus. A walking or touring holiday is easier with a car, a taxi for linear walks, or a mix of all three. This guide covers each option with fares from official sources as of November 2026.

Car, bus or both?

If you stay in Funchal and plan to visit the Old Town, the gardens and Câmara de Lobos, buses and the occasional taxi are enough. If you want sunrise at Pico do Arieiro, early starts at mountain trailheads or a loop of the north coast, hire a car for at least part of the trip. Many visitors do both: a few car-free days in town, then a car for the countryside.

SIGA: the regional bus network

Public buses on Madeira island run under one network brand, SIGA, operated by three companies: Horários do Funchal, SIGA Rodoeste and CAM (Companhia de Autocarros da Madeira). GIRO tickets can be used across the network, subject to the ticket type purchased; the Aerobus has its own ticket. Timetables are on the official SIGA site run by the regional government.

Fares as of November 2026

The fare table published by SIGA, under Portaria n.º 128/2026 of 23 March, splits trips into Municipal and Intermunicipal fares:

  • Ticket bought on board: €2.05 municipal, €2.65 intermunicipal.
  • Prepaid trip on a GIRO card: €1.45 municipal, €2.00 intermunicipal. The GIRO ticket card itself costs €0.50.
  • Day tickets: 1 day €4.95 municipal or €6.55 intermunicipal; 3 days €12.50 or €16.70; 7 days €23.50 or €31.10. Two-day and five-day versions also exist.
  • Regional Tourist tickets: a separate column in the table at €13.75 for 1 day, €23.00 for 3 days and €36.00 for 7 days.
  • Children aged 6 to 12 pay roughly half on each ticket type.

The prepaid GIRO card pays for itself after a handful of trips. Ask at an official sales point, listed on the SIGA site, which ticket covers the routes you plan to use before buying a multi-day or Regional Tourist ticket.

What buses do well, and what they do not

Town services in Funchal are frequent, and buses run along the south coast to places such as Caniço, Ribeira Brava and Machico. Services thin out on the north coast and to high trailheads, and some mountain areas see only a few buses a day. Check the official timetable for both the outward and return trip before relying on a bus to reach a walk. Our levada walks guide covers trailhead logistics.

From the airport: Aerobus, taxi or car

Madeira Airport is at Santa Cruz, east of Funchal. The Aerobus, operated by CAM, runs from the airport through central Funchal to Praia Formosa in the west of the city, stopping near many hotels. The timetable in force since 1 April 2026 shows the full run taking about 50 minutes, with departures from the airport roughly every 30 to 60 minutes from early morning to 23:00, plus a few night departures. There is no service on Christmas Day.

The SIGA fare table lists a prepaid Aerobus ticket at €5.55 (€2.75 for children aged 6 to 12), valid only on the Aerobus, as of November 2026. The Aerobus route sheet says payment on board is cash only. Times and stops are on the SIGA Aerobus page.

Taxis also serve the airport. See our airport guide for the terminal and Porto Santo Airport for the smaller island.

Taxis and ride-hailing

Licensed taxis are easy to find in Funchal at ranks along the seafront and outside the main hotels, and in smaller towns at a central rank. Taxis are also the practical answer for linear walks, where you start at one trailhead and finish at another. Agree the fare or ask for the meter before you set off on a long trip.

Bolt operates in Madeira: its official city page lists standard cars, XL vehicles for up to six people, and local taxis booked through the app, with the note that the taxi service is provided by an independent taxi operator and the in-app price is an estimate. Uber's official Madeira Airport page also offers UberX rides to and from the airport. Check the apps for live availability and pickup instructions.

Car hire: steep roads and tunnels

Driving is on the right. A fast expressway with many tunnels links the airport, Funchal and the main south-coast towns, and tunnels have shortened many routes to the north. Off the expressway, expect:

  • Steep gradients. Streets in Funchal and mountain roads can be very steep. A car with enough power and an automatic gearbox is worth considering if you are not confident with hill starts.
  • Tunnels. Many are long and some old ones are narrow and unlit. Turn on headlights and take sunglasses off before you enter.
  • Weather. Cloud and rain can close in fast on the high roads to Pico do Arieiro, Paul da Serra and Encumeada. Allow extra time and drive to the conditions.
  • Narrow village lanes. In places such as Jardim do Mar and Paul do Mar, park outside and walk in.

Parking at the busiest viewpoints and trailheads fills early. As of November 2026, the IFCN's 2026 price list sets parking at the Pico do Areeiro viewpoint at €4 per hour, first 30 minutes free, daily maximum €20, and at Queimadas at €2 per hour, first 30 minutes free, with a €10 daily cap. Cabo Girão has a separate viewpoint admission charge of €5 per adult as of November 2026, with exemptions for children aged 12 and under, Madeira residents and people with reduced mobility or using wheelchairs. This is an admission fee, not a parking tariff; check local parking signs. Our trail fees and tourist tax guide lists every visitor charge.

Parking in Funchal

Central Funchal has paid street parking and several underground car parks. Street spaces are scarce in the Old Town and near the Mercado dos Lavradores. If your hotel offers parking, it is often easier to leave the car there for town days and use it only for trips out. We did not find a current official municipal parking tariff to quote, so check the signs or the meter where you park.

Cable cars as transport

Several cable cars save a steep climb and double as sightseeing:

  • Funchal to Monte: from the seafront near the Old Town up to Monte, for the Monte Palace Tropical Garden and the toboggan ride back down.
  • Achadas da Cruz: a steep drop to the fields and shore below the cliffs in the far north-west, near Porto Moniz.

Each cable car is run by its own operator and sets its own prices and hours; check them on the day, as services can stop in high wind.

Getting to Porto Santo

By ferry

The Lobo Marinho ferry, run by Porto Santo Line, sails between Funchal and Porto Santo. The company states the crossing takes about 2 hours 15 minutes. The ship carries up to 1,153 passengers and 145 cars, has first-class and tourist-class seating, and passengers must be at the terminal at least 30 minutes before departure (one hour with a car). Bring photo ID: it is checked at boarding.

Fares vary with the season, the length of stay and the number of people, and there are combined packages with a car or hotel. The company's FAQ says children up to 4 travel free (but still need a ticket) and children up to 11 get 50% off. Tickets bought online are non-refundable. Timetables by month are published on the company's booking site; check the dates you want, as the sailing pattern changes through the year.

By air

Scheduled flights link Madeira Airport with Porto Santo Airport. Binter's official Madeira to Porto Santo page advertises morning and afternoon flights and a flight time of 25 minutes as of November 2026. Check the airline for your dates and fare. Flying is the quicker option; the ferry lets you take a car and is the classic day out. Our Porto Santo day trip page and Porto Santo travel guide cover what to do once you arrive, starting with the long sandy Porto Santo beach.

Putting it together

For a first trip, many people base themselves in Funchal, use buses and cable cars for the city, then hire a car for two or three days to see the west, the north coast and the mountains. Our five-day and seven-day itineraries follow that pattern, and where to stay in Madeira compares bases. The transport planning page has a short summary for quick reference.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the bus in Madeira?

As of November 2026, a SIGA ticket bought on board costs €2.05 for a municipal trip or €2.65 for an intermunicipal one. Prepaid trips on a GIRO card cost €1.45 or €2.00, and the card costs €0.50. Day tickets start at €4.95.

How do I get from Madeira Airport to Funchal?

The Aerobus runs from the airport through central Funchal to Praia Formosa in about 50 minutes end to end. A prepaid ticket costs €5.55 as of November 2026, and the route sheet says on-board payment is cash only. Taxis and hire cars are available at the terminal.

Is there Uber or Bolt in Madeira?

Bolt operates in Madeira, with standard cars, XL vehicles and local taxis bookable in the app. Uber also advertises UberX rides to and from Madeira Airport; check the apps for current availability.

Is it hard to drive in Madeira?

The expressway is straightforward, but mountain roads are steep and winding, many tunnels are long, and weather changes fast on high ground. Confident drivers manage well; take it slowly on the first day and consider an automatic.

How long is the ferry to Porto Santo?

Porto Santo Line states the Lobo Marinho crossing takes about 2 hours 15 minutes. Arrive at least 30 minutes before departure, or one hour with a car, and bring photo ID.

Can I reach hiking trailheads by bus?

Some, but services to the mountains are infrequent. Check the SIGA timetable for both directions before you go, or use a taxi, tour or hire car for early starts and linear walks.

guides.title: Madeira for First-Timers: What to Know Before You Go
guides.summary: Everything a first visit to Madeira needs: island layout, trip length, hire car or SIGA buses, wind at the airport, euros, plugs, trail fees and booking, tourist tax and entry rules.
guides.html:
Madeira is easy to visit and easy to misjudge. It looks small on a map, yet the mountains in its centre turn short distances into long, winding drives, and the weather on the north coast can be completely different from the sunshine in Funchal. This guide covers the basics a first-time visitor needs: how the island fits together, how long to stay, whether to hire a car, what to expect at the airport, and the rules that changed recently for walkers. Prices and rules below were read on official pages and are given as of November 2026.

How the island is laid out

Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal, made up of two inhabited islands, Madeira and Porto Santo, plus the uninhabited Desertas and Selvagens. Think of the main island in five parts:

  • Funchal and the south coast: the capital Funchal, the fishing town of Câmara de Lobos and the resort area of Caniço. There are hotels, restaurants and bus connections here.
  • West Madeira: Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol and Calheta, on the south-west coast, with the Paul da Serra plateau and the Rabaçal levadas above.
  • The north coast: Porto Moniz, São Vicente and Santana, greener and wetter, with lava pools and the laurel forest.
  • East Madeira: Machico and Caniçal, close to the airport, with the bare headland of Ponta de São Lourenço.
  • The central mountains: the peaks of Pico do Areeiro and Pico Ruivo, the highest point of the archipelago at 1,862 metres.

Porto Santo lies 71 km from Madeira according to its ferry operator, and is a separate trip with its own long sandy beach. Our destinations hub describes every area.

How many days you need

Three days covers Funchal, Monte and one mountain or coast day, and suits a city break; the 3-day itinerary shows how. Five to seven days is the sweet spot for a first visit, with time for the north coast, two or three levada walks and a spare day for weather; see the 5-day and 7-day itineraries. With ten days you can add Porto Santo, as in the 10-day itinerary. Walkers often want the full week on foot.

Car or no car

A hire car makes the north coast, the high viewpoints and the trailheads far easier, especially for sunrise at Pico do Areeiro. Madeira drives on the right. Roads are well built, with long tunnels on the main routes, but the older roads are steep and narrow, and parking in central Funchal is tight. Pick a smaller car and a hotel with parking.

Without a car, the regional bus network, SIGA, links Funchal with the rest of the island. Its official site names three operators, Companhia de Autocarros da Madeira, Siga Rodoeste and Horários do Funchal, managed by TiiM. Since January 2026 SIGA has sold visitor tickets loaded on the GIRO card, including day tickets for one, two, three, five or seven days and a regional tourist ticket that also covers the Aerobus airport service. Buses work well for Funchal and the south coast; the north coast and trailheads need more planning or an organised tour. Our getting around guide and transport page have the details.

The airport and its wind

A main arrival point is Cristiano Ronaldo Madeira International Airport (FNC) in Santa Cruz, on the east side of the island. The runway sits between cliffs and the sea, and strong winds are its weak point. Allow for weather disruption, and check your airline's advice if your flight is delayed or diverted. Porto Santo airport (PXO) serves the other inhabited island.

What this means for you: book travel insurance that covers delays, keep important plans off your arrival and departure days, avoid tight onward connections, and check your airline's app on the morning you fly. Ask your accommodation about any tourist-tax exemption if an unexpected delay extends your stay.

Money

Madeira uses the euro. The tourism board notes that card payments are accepted in most establishments, but carry some cash for small cafés, market stalls and parking machines in the hills.

Language, time and plugs

  • Language: Portuguese. English is widely understood in hotels, restaurants and tourist services, and a few words of Portuguese (obrigado or obrigada for thank you) are appreciated.
  • Time zone: the same as mainland Portugal and the UK: UTC in winter and UTC+1 in summer, with clocks going forward in March and back in October.
  • Electricity: European-standard sockets. Portugal's national tourism board lists 230/400 V, 50 Hz, with 230 V for household devices. Visitors from the UK, Ireland and the USA need a plug adapter, and North American devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.
  • Emergencies: call 112. See our emergency contacts page.

Tap water

The official tourism website describes tap water as safe to drink. Follow any local water notice and ask your accommodation if you are unsure about its supply.

Tipping

Tipping is not compulsory. Leaving some change or rounding up after a good meal is a personal choice rather than an expectation, so tip when service earns it.

Trail fees and booking

This is the change most first-timers miss. Classified walking trails (PR routes) managed by the regional forestry institute, IFCN, now require a booked entry slot and, for visitors, a fee, paid only online through the SIMplifica portal. As of November 2026 the IFCN fee list for visitors is:

  • €4.50 for an individual trail (except PR1);
  • €4.50 for PR1 up to the Pedra Rija viewpoint, and €10.50 for the full PR1 once it reopens;
  • €9.00 for two or more trails in one day, €22.50 for three days and €52.50 for seven days (PR1 excluded).

The multi-day rates are a discount, not a pass: you still book each trail and slot. Children aged 12 or under, Madeira residents with proof, and people with a disability of at least 60% with one accompanying legal guardian do not pay but still register. IFCN also exempts qualifying property-rights holders exercising those rights and essential-service personnel on duty from both booking and payment. Refunds or rescheduling apply only when the authorities close or restrict a trail. Trails are closed and reopened often after storms and fires: in November 2026 the IFCN operational notice read on 16 November 2026 listed both the full Pico do Areeiro to Pico Ruivo route (PR1) and the section to Pedra Rija as closed, while PR6 and PR9 were open. Check the IFCN trail-status page on the day. Read our trail fees and tourist tax guide and the levada walks guide before you plan walks.

The tourist tax

A municipal tourist tax can be collected by your accommodation, depending on where you stay. In Funchal, as of November 2026, the council's notice sets it at €2 per person per night up to a maximum of seven nights, with guests aged 12 or under, Madeira residents and people with a disability of 60% or more exempt. Check the current local rate and exemptions with your accommodation when you book.

As of November 2026, entry to the Cabo Girão viewpoint costs €5 for non-residents over 12; children aged 12 or under and Madeira residents are exempt. This is separate from trail fees.

Entry rules

Madeira is part of Portugal, so EU and Schengen rules apply. EU citizens travel with a valid passport or national identity card. Most visitors from the UK, USA, Canada and Australia can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen area without a visa. The EU's Entry/Exit System (EES) registers eligible non-EU visitors electronically at the external border in place of passport stamps. Biometric checks can include fingerprints and a photo; exemptions apply, including for residents and young children's fingerprints. Check the official EU ETIAS website before departure for the current travel-authorisation requirements. Our visa requirements page has more, and your own government's travel advice is the final word.

Common first-timer mistakes

  • Judging the island by Funchal's weather. The south is usually warmer and drier; the north and the mountains get more wind and rain. Check the weather page and webcams before driving up.
  • Turning up at a trailhead without a booking. Walking a classified IFCN trail without a valid booking can lead to a fine.
  • Expecting long sandy beaches on the main island. Madeira has pebble beaches, lidos and lava pools, as well as sandy beaches at places such as Seixal, Machico and Calheta; Porto Santo has a much longer sandy beach. See our beaches and pools guide.
  • Packing too much into one day. Driving times are longer than distances suggest.
  • Leaving no slack for the airport. Wind delays are part of life here.
  • Forgetting layers. It can be warm in Funchal and cold and misty at 1,800 metres on the same morning.

For seasons, read the best time to visit Madeira and, for a winter trip, Madeira in winter. When you know what you want to see, things to do in Madeira and where to stay will help you build the trip. Our local tips fill in the rest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Madeira a country?

No. Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal, part of the EU and the Schengen area, made up of Madeira, Porto Santo and the uninhabited Desertas and Selvagens islands.

Do I need to hire a car in Madeira?

Not for Funchal and the south coast, which SIGA buses serve well. For the north coast, sunrise on the peaks and most trailheads, a car saves a lot of time. Madeira drives on the right.

What happens if my flight cannot land because of wind?

Follow your airline's instructions about delays, diversions or cancellations. Keep your arrival day light and carry insurance that covers delays.

How much are trail fees in Madeira?

As of November 2026, IFCN charges visitors €4.50 for an individual classified trail and €10.50 for the full PR1 once it reopens, with combined rates of €9.00 a day, €22.50 for three days and €52.50 for seven. Book every trail on SIMplifica.

Is there a tourist tax in Madeira?

In Funchal, the council notice gives €2 per person per night for up to seven nights, with children aged 12 or under exempt, as of November 2026. Your accommodation collects it; confirm the rate when booking.

Do I need ETIAS to visit Madeira?

Check the official EU ETIAS website before you travel. As of November 2026, the European Commission states that ETIAS is not in operation and is not collecting applications. Check again before departure.

guides.budget: Moderate: plan for car hire or bus tickets, trail fees and the nightly tourist tax on top of meals and activities

guides.title: Madeira in Winter: December to February Guide
guides.summary: Winter in Funchal means mean highs of about 20C, lows of about 14C and a sea near 18 to 20C, with at least 1 mm of rain on about six to nine days a month at Funchal Observatory. The peaks can see snow and ice, and storms close trails, so plan walks day by day.
guides.html:
Is Madeira a good winter destination?

For winter sun with a jacket in the bag, yes. For guaranteed beach weather, no. From December to February the south coast around Funchal stays mild by day, the sea is cool but swimmable for many northern Europeans, and the city is at its most festive from early December to early January. In exchange you get more rain, shorter days, cold and sometimes snowy summits, and walking trails that open and close with the weather.

The air-temperature and rainfall figures below use IPMA (Portugal's weather and climate institute) 1991 to 2020 climate normals for a named station; the sea figures are our calculations from its monthly observations. They are averages, not forecasts. For the rest of the year, see our best time to visit guide.

Winter weather by station

Funchal and Porto Santo have full monthly normals. For Santana and Chão do Areeiro, the January values are worked out from IPMA's January 2026 regional bulletin as observation minus anomaly; a complete monthly table for those two stations was not found, so the other months are left blank rather than guessed. Chão do Areeiro is an upland station below the summit of Pico do Arieiro; the summit itself is higher and more exposed. A 1991 to 2020 sheet for Santa Catarina airport was not found in this check.

The figures tell the winter story clearly. December is Funchal's wettest month of the year on average. The north coast around Santana is about four degrees cooler than Funchal in January and noticeably wetter. In the uplands a January day averages under 9C, with more than three times Funchal's rain. Porto Santo is a little cooler than Funchal by day, with rain on more days but less of it in total.

Sea temperature in winter

At Funchal's Pontinha harbour station, the IPMA series published by DREM, the regional statistics office, gives average sea temperatures of 20.1C in December, 18.9C in January and 18.2C in February for 1991 to 2020 (our averages of the monthly means). The water is coolest in late winter and early spring, at about 18C in February and March. That is cooler than most people like for a long swim, though hardy swimmers still go in on calm days at places such as the Lido bathing complex or Praia Formosa; check what is open and supervised before you go. Winter swells are more common, so follow the flags and lifeguard advice, and be careful at Doca do Cavacas and the Porto Moniz natural pools when the sea is rough.

Walking in winter: closures, fees and bookings

Winter is a fine time to walk in Madeira when the weather allows. The Laurisilva laurel forest is lush and the levadas run full. But storms can also close trails, and some routes stay closed for long periods after storm or fire damage. On 16 November 2026, IFCN's operational notice listed classified routes or route sections as closed, including both PR1 Vereda do Areeiro options (the full route and the section to Pedra Rija) and PR13 Vereda do Fanal. These lists change week to week.

The rules as of November 2026, from the official IFCN pages:

  • Fees. Non-residents pay 4.50 euros for an individual classified trail and 10.50 euros for the full PR1 from Pico do Arieiro to Pico Ruivo. Residents with proof of residence, children aged 12 and under, and people with a disability of at least 60% with one accompanying legal guardian are exempt.
  • Bookings. Visitors must reserve each trail and time slot in advance on the Simplifica portal, including children and residents exempt from payment. Qualifying property-rights holders exercising those rights and essential-service personnel on duty are exempt from both booking and payment. IFCN says bookings are made only online.
  • Weather. IFCN states that weather warnings do not automatically close every classified trail; closures are decided route by route. Separately, the regional civil protection service advises against activities in exposed mountain and coastal areas while warnings are in force.
  • Status. Check the IFCN trail-status page on the day, not the week before.

Good winter choices are lower, sheltered routes on days with a settled forecast. Our levada walks guide and trail fees guide explain the routes and the booking steps, and the levada walks page lists the main options, including Levada das 25 Fontes and Levada do Caldeirão Verde.

Snow and ice on the peaks

Snow does fall on Madeira's highest ground in some winters. IPMA's January 2026 bulletin describes precipitation falling at times as snow, and the regional roads authority has closed the ER 202 between Poiso and Pico do Arieiro because of snow. There is no fixed date or threshold: the road and the summit can be open and clear one day and shut the next. If your heart is set on sunrise at Pico do Arieiro or the Pico do Arieiro to Pico Ruivo hike, keep two or three possible days in the plan, carry gloves and a warm hat, and never walk the ridge in ice, high wind or poor visibility. The plateau around Fanal is also cold and often misty in winter.

Christmas lights and the festive season

The festive season is the best reason to choose December. The official calendar schedules the general illumination of the Funchal amphitheatre from 1 December 2026 to 10 January 2027, and the city centre fills with lights, music and stalls; see our Christmas in Funchal page. Two local traditions are worth planning around:

  • Missas do Parto. From 15 December, parishes hold nine early-morning Masses before Christmas, followed by celebrations in the churchyard.
  • Market Night (Noite do Mercado). On the evening of 23 December, residents do their last Christmas shopping at the Mercado dos Lavradores and the streets around it.

A large nativity scene covers the fountain at Largo da Restauração, and the season closes with the Chants of Epiphany in the Municipal Gardens on 5 January 2027. On public holidays such as Christmas Day and 26 December, a regional holiday, check each operator: as of November 2026 SIGA Rodoeste lists no journeys on 25 December 2026 and Sunday timetables on 26 December 2026; our public holidays guide lists the dates.

New Year's Eve fireworks

The fireworks over Funchal bay on 31 December are the high point of the winter. Visit Madeira notes that the display was classed by Guinness World Records as the world's largest fireworks display on the 2006 to 2007 New Year's Eve and kept the record until 2012, and describes a show of about eight minutes. As of November 2026 the official start time and launch points for the 2026 to 2027 display had not been published on the pages we checked. Rooms with a view of the bay are booked far ahead, and roads and buses are busy after midnight. Read our New Year fireworks guide and the fireworks event page for viewpoints and planning.

February: Carnival and the run into spring

The Madeira Carnival runs in downtown Funchal from 3 to 14 February 2027, with the allegorical parade on 5 and 6 February and the slapstick parade on 9 February. Carnival Tuesday falls on 9 February 2027. It is an optional holiday under Portugal's Labour Code; the regional government gave its staff time off on Carnival Tuesday in 2026.

Good things to do on a winter trip

  • Gardens: the Madeira Botanical Garden, Monte Palace Tropical Garden and Palheiro Gardens are green all year.
  • Monte by cable car, then down by toboggan.
  • Wet-day options: the Blandy's Wine Lodge, a Madeira wine tasting and the painted doors of Funchal's old town.
  • Warming food for cool evenings: carne de vinha d'alhos, sopa de trigo and a slice of bolo de mel, the honey cake.
  • Sea trips such as whale and dolphin watching when the forecast is calm.

What not to expect

  • Beach heat. Highs near 20C on the south coast are pleasant, not hot, and the sea is at its coolest.
  • Dry weeks. At Funchal Observatory, at least 1 mm of rain falls on about six to nine days a month in winter on average, more in the north and the mountains.
  • Every trail open. Check for closures after bad weather; some routes can stay shut for long periods.
  • A clear summit on a set day. Cloud, ice or snow can close the road or hide the view.
  • A time difference from the UK. Madeira keeps the same time as mainland Portugal and the UK: UTC in winter.

Base yourself on the south coast, in Funchal, Caniço or Calheta, for the driest winter weather; our where to stay guide compares the options. Check the weather page for the full station notes.

Frequently Asked Questions

How warm is Madeira in January?

Funchal's January normal is a mean daily high of 20.0C and a low of 14.3C. The north coast is cooler (16.1C at Santana) and the uplands much colder: Chão do Areeiro averages a high of 8.7C and a low of 2.8C.

Can you swim in Madeira in winter?

Some do. The Funchal harbour series averages 20.1C in December, 18.9C in January and 18.2C in February. Choose a supervised bathing place on a calm day and follow the flags.

Does it snow in Madeira?

Snow can fall on high ground. IPMA recorded precipitation falling at times as snow in January 2026, and the road between Poiso and Pico do Arieiro has been closed because of snow.

Are the levada walks open in winter?

Some are, but check for weather-related closures. Book each classified trail on Simplifica, pay the fee unless exempt (4.50 euros for most trails as of November 2026), and check IFCN's trail-status page on the morning you walk.

When do the Christmas lights go on in Funchal?

The official calendar schedules the illumination from 1 December 2026 to 10 January 2027. The switch-on time had not been published when we checked.

Is Madeira busy over Christmas and New Year?

Yes. Book accommodation early if you want a room facing the bay on 31 December. For a quieter trip, consider January after the holidays; early February 2027 overlaps Carnival.

What should I pack for Madeira in winter?

Light layers for the coast, a waterproof jacket, a warm fleece, a hat and gloves for the mountains, and walking shoes with good grip for wet paths.
guides.bestTime: Early December for the lights before the holiday rush, or January after the holidays for quiet walking
guides.budget: Allow extra for Christmas, New Year and Carnival; compare accommodation prices for your dates

guides.title: Madeira Levada Walks: Trails, Fees, Booking and Safety
guides.summary: Madeira's classified PR trails need a booked slot and, for non-residents over 12, a fee from €4.50. Trail status, distances, gear and trailhead logistics as of November 2026.
guides.html:
Madeira's levadas are irrigation channels that carry water from the wet, high interior to farms and towns lower down. The maintenance paths beside them are now used for walking: mostly gentle gradients, laurel forest, waterfalls and long views. They are also mountain paths with drops, tunnels and fast-changing weather, so a little planning matters. This guide covers the official trail network, how to choose a walk, the fee and booking system that applies to non-residents, what to carry and how to reach the trailheads. Fees and trail status below are as of November 2026 and come from the regional forestry and nature institute (IFCN) and the official tourism board.

What levadas and PR trails are

Not every path beside a channel is an official trail. The region keeps a list of classified walking routes, each with a PR number (from Pequena Rota, short route), waymarking and an information panel at the start. Some follow levadas, others are veredas (mountain footpaths) or old royal roads. The IFCN manages most of them; a few are managed by a municipality or parish council, and the official list names the manager for each.

The fee and booking system covers classified trails managed by the IFCN and included in that regime. Other managers may have different arrangements. The IFCN says plainly that it cannot recommend unclassified paths, because it does not maintain or check them. If you follow a route you found online that is not on the PR list, you are on your own for its condition.

Many of the classic walks run through the Laurisilva laurel forest and the wider Madeira Natural Park, so expect wet rock, moss and roots underfoot even on easy sections. Our levada walks overview sums up the experience if you are still deciding whether to walk at all.

Choosing a walk: fitness and vertigo

Three questions narrow it down quickly.

  • How far and how long? Distances below are one-way unless stated; the tourism board supplies the walking-time estimates. Many levada walks are out-and-back, so double the distance.
  • How much up and down? Levada paths are close to level; veredas climb. Ponta de São Lourenço sits near sea level; the central peaks are above 1,800 m.
  • How do you handle drops? Several levadas have sections where the path is narrow with a steep fall on one side, sometimes protected by a fence, sometimes not. If you have vertigo, start with a short forest walk such as Balcões and judge from there.

The tourism board grades the walks listed below as easy or medium. Treat "medium" as a real walk: proper footwear, water and a few hours of steady effort.

The best-known walks, with official figures

Distances are from the IFCN trail table; times and grades are from the official tourism board's trail pages. Status is the IFCN listing read on 16 November 2026.

  • PR6 Levada das 25 Fontes (Rabaçal, west of the central plateau): 4.3 km plus 4.3 km back, about 3 hours, medium. Listed open by IFCN. Its table describes one-way circulation via a bypass, but the tourism board currently notes temporary two-way operation. Follow current signs and official instructions. Our 25 Fontes walk page has more detail.
  • PR6.1 Levada do Risco: a shorter walk from the same Rabaçal start to the Risco waterfall, graded easy, open. The IFCN table lists 3 km plus 3 km back, while the tourism board page gives 1.5 km one way, so allow for the longer figure.
  • PR9 Levada do Caldeirão Verde (from Queimadas Forest Park near Santana): 8.7 km to Caldeirão do Inferno plus 8.7 km back, about 6 hours 30 minutes, medium, with tunnels where a torch is essential. Open. Start at Queimadas and see our Caldeirão Verde page.
  • PR11 Vereda dos Balcões (Ribeiro Frio): 1.5 km plus 1.5 km back, about 1 hour 30 minutes, easy. Open. It ends at the Balcões viewpoint, a short introduction to levada walking.
  • PR8 Vereda da Ponta de São Lourenço (east tip, near Caniçal): 4 km plus 4 km back, about 2 hours 30 minutes, medium. Open. Follow the signed temporary diversions noted by the tourism board. Exposed, treeless and hot or windy; details on our Ponta de São Lourenço page.
  • PR18 Levada do Rei (north coast, São Jorge): 5.3 km plus 5.3 km back, about 3 hours 30 minutes, medium. Open.
  • PR1.2 Vereda do Pico Ruivo (Achada do Teixeira): 2.8 km plus 2.8 km back, about 1 hour 30 minutes, medium. Listed open, and an official way up Pico Ruivo, the island's highest summit.
  • PR1 Vereda do Areeiro (from Pico do Arieiro towards Pico Ruivo): 6.1 km, about 3 hours, medium. Listed as closed on the IFCN table read on 16 November 2026; see the next section.

For a wheelchair or buggy, the IFCN lists two adapted routes signed "Um Caminho para todos" (a path for everyone): PR6.8 Levada do Paul II (1.2 km, about 30 minutes) and PR9.1 at Queimadas (1.9 km). Both were listed passable in the IFCN operational notice read on 16 November 2026. The tourism board also marks PR6.8 open, but marks PR9.1 closed. Confirm current conditions with IFCN before using either adapted route.

Official trail status today

Trails close after storms, rockfalls and fires, and reopen in stages. On the IFCN table read on 16 November 2026, these well-known routes were listed as closed: PR1 Vereda do Areeiro, PR1.3 Vereda da Encumeada, PR2 Vereda do Urzal, PR3 Vereda do Burro, PR4 Levada do Barreiro, PR7 Levada do Moinho, PR10 Levada do Furado, PR13 Vereda do Fanal, PR14 Levada dos Cedros, PR16 Levada Fajã do Rodrigues and PR17 Caminho do Pináculo e Folhadal, among others. Some closed routes carry notes about a passable stretch. The PR1 table retains a two-way note for Pedra Rija, but the IFCN operational notice explicitly lists both PR1 options, including the section to Pedra Rija, as closed. A listed fee is not permission to enter a closed route.

The IFCN FAQ adds that the whole of PR1 reopened on 1 May 2026, that the section beyond Pedra Rija runs one way only towards Pico Ruivo, and that walkers leave Pico Ruivo by PR1.1 or PR1.2. The status table now lists PR1 as closed again, so check the IFCN trail-status page and SIMplifica on the morning you walk, not the week before. Walking a closed trail is an offence under the regional trails law, with fines from €250 to €2,500 for an individual.

IFCN also says that a weather warning does not automatically close every trail: each closure is decided and published route by route. If a trail you booked is officially closed or restricted, you can ask the IFCN for a new date or a refund within 10 working days from the booking date, as its FAQ states.

The trail fee and slot booking

Since 1 January 2026, visitors using classified trails managed by the IFCN and covered by its booking regime need a booked entry slot, and non-residents normally pay a fee. The rules, as of November 2026, from the IFCN FAQ and Portaria n.º 801/2025 as amended by Portaria n.º 48/2026:

  • Single trail (except PR1): €4.50 per person over 12.
  • PR1 to the Pedra Rija viewpoint and back: €4.50.
  • Full PR1 (including PR1.1, PR1.2 and, when it reopens, PR1.3): €10.50.
  • Combined trails, excluding PR1: €9.00 for two or more in one day, €22.50 over three days, €52.50 over seven days. These are cheaper rates, not passes: you still book every trail and slot.
  • Exempt from paying (but still required to book): residents of the Autonomous Region of Madeira with proof, children aged 12 or under, and people with a disability of 60% or more plus one accompanying guardian, with proof.

Qualifying property-rights holders exercising those rights and essential-service personnel on duty are exempt from both booking and payment. Bookings are made only online, on the SIMplifica portal, the regional government's services site; you cannot pay at IFCN offices. You pick each trail, date and entry slot, and the system applies the cheapest combination at checkout. Same-day and next-day bookings are possible if places remain; slots close when full. The IFCN allows roughly 15 minutes either side of your slot. Payment problems go to the SIMplifica contact centre, not the IFCN. Book and pay before you leave your hotel: the tourism board warns that mobile coverage in the mountains can be poor.

Cancelling for your own reasons, including rain, illness or a missed flight, forfeits the fee. Walking a PR without a booking is an infraction and can lead to a fine. Our guide to trail fees and the tourist tax sets out every visitor charge in one place.

What to carry

  • Walking shoes or boots with real grip. Levada edges are often wet and mossy.
  • A headtorch for any walk with tunnels (PR9 and the Rabaçal routes have them), with spare batteries.
  • A waterproof jacket and a warm layer. The plateau and peaks are far cooler than Funchal.
  • Water and food beyond what you expect to need, sun protection, and a charged phone.
  • Your SIMplifica booking, saved offline.

The IFCN's own safety advice: do not walk alone, tell someone your route and return time, check the fire risk, and finish before dark.

Weather and the best time to walk

Weather on the north side and in the mountains can differ completely from the south coast on the same day. The IFCN advises against walking in heavy rain, strong wind, hail or snow. Check current forecasts and webcams before travelling to high viewpoints. Winter walking is popular, with cooler, wetter conditions up high; see when to visit Madeira, Madeira in winter and the weather page. In an emergency, call 112, and keep the emergency contacts on your phone.

Guided or self-guided

No classified trail requires a guide, the IFCN confirms, but walkers must still assess current conditions and follow the signs. A guide makes sense if you want transport between two ends of a linear route, if you are nervous about exposure, or if you want someone to explain the flora and history. Tour companies with an IFCN protocol book and pay at a different rate, so a guided price may already include the fee: ask before you also book on SIMplifica. Without a protocol, an operator's clients follow the same rules as individual walkers.

Buses and parking at trailheads

Most high trailheads are easiest by car or on a tour. The regional SIGA bus network does serve some walking areas, but services to the mountains are infrequent; plan with the official SIGA timetables before relying on a bus back. Our getting around Madeira guide covers buses, taxis and car hire.

The IFCN's price list, as of November 2026, includes parking charges at some forest-park car parks it runs: at Queimadas, €2 per hour with the first 30 minutes free and a €10 daily cap; at the Pico do Areeiro viewpoint, €4 per hour with the first 30 minutes free and a €20 daily cap. Linear walks need a plan for getting back to the car: the IFCN states it does not provide return transport from Pico Ruivo to Pico do Areeiro.

For a whole trip built around walking, see our seven-day hiking itinerary, and the destination guides for where to base yourself; Santana and Porto Moniz put you close to the north-coast trails.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I have to pay to walk the levadas in Madeira?

On classified PR trails managed by the IFCN, non-residents over 12 normally pay; the disability exemption described above also applies. As of November 2026 a single trail costs €4.50 per person and the full PR1 costs €10.50. Unclassified paths are not part of the system, but the IFCN does not maintain or recommend them.

Do I need to book a time slot?

Yes. Visitors, including children and residents who pay nothing, must register and book an entry slot for each classified IFCN trail covered by the regime on the SIMplifica portal. Qualifying property-rights holders and essential-service personnel exercising their rights or duties are exceptions. Same-day bookings are possible if places remain.

Can I get a refund if it rains?

No. The IFCN only reschedules or refunds when the trail is officially closed or restricted on your booking date. Requests must be made within 10 working days from the booking date, as the IFCN FAQ states.

Is the Pico do Arieiro to Pico Ruivo walk open?

On 16 November 2026, the IFCN operational notice listed both the full PR1 and the section to Pedra Rija as closed. Pico Ruivo itself was reachable by PR1.2 from Achada do Teixeira. Check the official status page on the day you plan to walk.

Which levada walk is best for beginners?

PR11 Vereda dos Balcões is graded easy and is 1.5 km each way, with an official estimated duration of 1 hour 30 minutes, ending at a viewpoint over the laurel forest. PR6.1 Levada do Risco is another easy option from Rabaçal.

Do I need a torch?

For any route with tunnels, yes. PR9 Caldeirão Verde and several Rabaçal walks pass through tunnels where a headtorch is essential.
