guides.duration: Half a day to a full day per walk
guides.budget: Trail fee from €4.50 per person per walk for non-residents over 12 (as of November 2026); transport and guiding extra

guides.title: Madeira New Year Fireworks: Where to Watch Over Funchal Bay
guides.summary: Funchal's midnight fireworks fill the whole bay for about eight minutes. The 2026/27 plan approves at least 59 launch posts. Where to watch, how the night runs and what the weather does, as of November 2026.
guides.html:
At midnight on 31 December, Funchal sets off fireworks from the seafront, from platforms in the bay and from dozens of sites up the hillside that the city climbs. The launch-site plan spans the bay and the hillside behind the city. Visit Madeira describes it as lasting about eight minutes, and Guinness World Records named it the world's largest fireworks display for New Year's Eve 2006 to 2007, a title it kept until 2012. Our event page for the Funchal New Year fireworks has the short version; this guide is for planning the night itself.

What is officially planned for 2026/27

The regional government decides where the fireworks are launched each year. For the 2026/27 New Year, Resolution 657/2026 of the Council of the Regional Government, published in the official journal (JORAM) on 7 July 2026, approves the plan of launch posts. It sets out:

  • 27 posts across the Funchal amphitheatre, the hillside that rises behind the city. Named sites include the lower level of the Lido fort, the Ponta Gorda and Barreirinha bathing complexes, the promenade at Praia Formosa, the lawn inside the Madeira Botanical Garden and the Pináculo viewpoint.
  • At least 25 posts along the seafront, on land or at sea, between the west end of Pier 8 (Cais 8) of the port and the pontoons at Praia do Almirante Reis, just east of the old town.
  • 5 posts on the sea: three south of the Pontinha breakwater and two between Pier 8 and the Lazareto.
  • 2 posts on Porto Santo, at the Portela viewpoint and at the south end of the old pier in Vila Baleira, so the smaller island has its own show (see our Porto Santo travel guide).

That makes at least 59 launch posts across Madeira and Porto Santo. As of November 2026, we could not confirm the detailed programme for the night (concerts, stages and timings around midnight). Check the regional government and Funchal city council announcements before you travel. The launch sites above are useful in one practical way: they are the places you will not be allowed to stand, because each post has a safety perimeter.

Where to watch from land

Check access arrangements for your chosen public viewing area. Pick the kind of view you want and how much crowd you can take.

The seafront

The waterfront between the marina, Avenida do Mar and Praça do Povo puts you closest to the seafront line of fireworks and to the bay platforms. Allow for crowds here. People start claiming space in the early evening, and leaving after midnight is slow. If you want this view, eat early, arrive early and accept that you will stay put. The Sé cathedral, the Mercado dos Lavradores and the old town are all a short walk inland, which helps if you want dinner nearby.

Parks and terraces above the centre

A little height lets you see the hillside posts and the bay together. For the 2024/25 New Year, the city council ran a free programme in Parque de Santa Catarina, west of the centre, from 20:30 to 03:00, with concerts, food stalls and a DJ after the fireworks. It is a good model for what the council organises, but it is not a promise for 2026/27: check the council's announcement in December.

The hillside neighbourhoods

Many residents watch from streets, balconies and terraces higher up the amphitheatre, where the whole bay is in view and the crowds are thinner. The catch is that some posts are on the same slopes, roads are restricted, and you need a plan to get back. Staying in a hotel or apartment with a bay-facing terrace is the easiest version of this.

Beyond Funchal

If you are staying in neighbouring Câmara de Lobos or Caniço, ask your accommodation whether its particular viewpoint has a clear view of Funchal's display before deciding to watch from there.

Watching from the sea

The fireworks are as much a sea event as a land one. If you are arriving by cruise ship, ask the cruise line where it will be positioned for the display and whether you can watch from on board.

If booking a New Year's Eve boat trip, ask for the licence, the boarding time, where the boat will hold position, what is included and what happens if the sea is rough. For a calmer look at the bay earlier in your stay, see whale and dolphin watching.

Road closures and public transport on the night

Expect the city centre to close to cars in the evening. We had not found the 2026/27 traffic plan as of November 2026, so here is what the council announced for a recent year, as a guide to the pattern:

  • For the 2024/25 New Year (announced on 30 December 2024), Funchal City Council restricted traffic and parking especially on Avenida do Mar and other parts of the downtown area between 20:00 and 02:00.
  • In the parishes of São Gonçalo, Monte, Santa Maria Maior, Santo António and São Martinho, traffic was not banned but was limited to one lane at varying times.

In practice, plan to walk the last part of the way in and the whole way out. If you are staying outside Funchal, park well away from the centre or use a taxi drop-off point on the edge of the restricted area. For buses, the urban operator Horários do Funchal and the island network SIGA publish any special New Year service themselves; we had not found a 2026/27 notice when we checked in November 2026. Our getting around Madeira guide and the transportation page explain the bus network, tickets and taxis. The Monte cable car is a daytime ride, not a way home after midnight.

Booking pressure

Book New Year accommodation early. Compare room prices and availability for your dates, especially if a bay view matters. Check flights into Madeira Airport and ask restaurants with a bay view about their New Year's Eve arrangements. If you cannot find a bay-view room, consider:

  • a room in the old town or near the marina, and walk to the seafront;
  • a base in Caniço or Câmara de Lobos, watching from there or taking a taxi in early;
  • a later trip: the festive season continues into January, and compare prices for your dates.

Our where to stay in Madeira guide compares the areas.

Before the fireworks: lights and Market Night

The fireworks mark New Year during a festive season that starts a month earlier. Visit Madeira gives the Christmas and New Year festivities as running from 1 December 2026 to 10 January 2027, and the official tourist calendar keeps the illumination of the Funchal amphitheatre on for the same dates. The lights go on at nightfall on 1 December.

On the evening of 23 December comes Market Night (Noite do Mercado), when thousands of residents do their last Christmas shopping at the Mercado dos Lavradores and carols are sung inside the market. Allow for crowds around the market. The official calendar lists the Chants of Epiphany on 5 January 2027 in the Municipal Gardens, while the tourism event page describes Praça do Povo. Confirm the venue in the final programme. See Christmas in Funchal for the full season.

Seasonal food is part of it: bolo de mel, the dark honey cake, and carne de vinha d'alhos appear on menus, and stalls pour poncha.

December weather and the fireworks

December in Funchal is mild but it is the wettest month of the year at the city's official station. IPMA's 1991 to 2020 climate normals for the Funchal Observatory give a mean daily maximum of 21.0°C and a mean minimum of 15.5°C in December, with 94.8 mm of rain on an average of 8.6 days of at least 1 mm. Midnight on the seafront feels cooler than those figures suggest once you have been standing for a few hours, so bring a light jacket and something waterproof. See the Madeira weather page for every month.

Do not assume the show or your access route will remain available in bad weather. If a weather warning is issued, follow official instructions, and in an emergency call 112 (see emergency contacts).

A simple plan for the night

  1. Have a late lunch and an early dinner; restaurants near the seafront fill fast.
  2. Be in place by about 22:00 if you want the seafront, later if you have a terrace.
  3. Carry cash, water, a jacket and a charged phone; meet-up points are hard to find in the crowd.
  4. After midnight, wait 30 to 60 minutes before moving if you are not in a hurry, and walk rather than queue for a taxi.
  5. On 1 January, which is a public holiday, expect some shops and services to be closed (see Madeira public holidays 2027).

If you are planning a longer winter trip, Madeira in winter covers walking and weather, and the 5-day itinerary fits easily around New Year.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time do the Madeira New Year fireworks start, and how long do they last?

The fireworks start at midnight on 31 December. Visit Madeira describes the display as lasting about eight minutes, as a general description rather than a confirmed 2026/27 duration.

Do you need a ticket to watch the fireworks in Funchal?

Check access restrictions for public streets and the seafront, and any park programme separately. Boat trips, cruises, restaurants and accommodation have their own charges.

Where is the best place to watch the fireworks in Funchal?

The seafront between the marina and Praça do Povo offers a waterfront view; allow for crowds. A terrace or park higher up, such as Parque de Santa Catarina, shows the hillside launch points and the bay together. Avoid the launch sites themselves, which have safety perimeters.

Are roads closed in Funchal on New Year's Eve?

Yes, expect restrictions. For 2024/25 the council restricted traffic and parking on Avenida do Mar and in the downtown area from 20:00 to 02:00, with single-lane traffic in several hillside parishes. We had not found the 2026/27 plan as of November 2026.

Can you see the New Year fireworks from Porto Santo?

Porto Santo has its own launch posts in the 2026/27 plan, at the Portela viewpoint and the old pier in Vila Baleira. Funchal's display is too far away to watch properly from Porto Santo.
guides.budget: Allow for seasonal demand; book rooms and flights early

guides.title: Madeira Public Holidays 2027: Full Calendar
guides.summary: Madeira has 16 public holidays in 2027: Portugal's 13 national holidays plus three regional ones (2 April, 1 July and 26 December). Funchal adds its city holiday on Saturday 21 August. Good Friday is 26 March and Easter Sunday 28 March.
guides.html:
The 2027 calendar in brief

Public holidays in Madeira come from three layers of law. Portugal's Labour Code (Código do Trabalho, article 234) sets 13 mandatory national holidays. The regional government adds three holidays that apply across the autonomous region, on Madeira island and on Porto Santo alike. Each municipality then has its own local holiday, observed under the applicable employment agreement or contract within that municipality. Easter, Good Friday and Corpus Christi move each year; the dates below are confirmed against the Lisbon Astronomical Observatory's table of movable feasts, and every weekday has been checked against the 2027 calendar.

In 2027 that gives 16 national and regional holidays, plus the local holiday where you are staying. Six of the 16 fall on a Saturday or Sunday.

National and regional holidays in 2027

DateWeekdayHolidayApplies to
1 JanuaryFridayNew Year's Day (Ano Novo)All of Portugal
26 MarchFridayGood Friday (Sexta-Feira Santa)All of Portugal
28 MarchSundayEaster Sunday (Domingo de Páscoa)All of Portugal
2 AprilFridayAutonomy Day (Dia da Autonomia)Madeira region
25 AprilSundayFreedom Day (Dia da Liberdade)All of Portugal
1 MaySaturdayLabour Day (Dia do Trabalhador)All of Portugal
27 MayThursdayCorpus Christi (Corpo de Deus)All of Portugal
10 JuneThursdayPortugal Day (Dia de Portugal, de Camões e das Comunidades Portuguesas)All of Portugal
1 JulyThursdayMadeira Day (Dia da Região Autónoma da Madeira e das Comunidades Madeirenses)Madeira region
15 AugustSundayAssumption (Assunção de Nossa Senhora)All of Portugal
5 OctoberTuesdayRepublic Day (Implantação da República)All of Portugal
1 NovemberMondayAll Saints' Day (Dia de Todos os Santos)All of Portugal
1 DecemberWednesdayRestoration of Independence (Restauração da Independência)All of Portugal
8 DecemberWednesdayImmaculate Conception (Imaculada Conceição)All of Portugal
25 DecemberSaturdayChristmas Day (Natal)All of Portugal
26 DecemberSundayRegional holiday, the day after ChristmasMadeira region

The national holidays

Article 234 of the Labour Code lists the mandatory holidays as 1 January, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, 25 April, 1 May, Corpus Christi, 10 June, 15 August, 5 October, 1 November, 1 December, 8 December and 25 December. The wording of the current list comes from Law 8/2016. Easter Monday and Carnival Tuesday are not on it.

The movable dates for 2027, from the Lisbon Astronomical Observatory (OAL):

  • Carnival Tuesday: 9 February 2027 (not a statutory holiday; see below)
  • Good Friday: 26 March 2027
  • Easter Sunday: 28 March 2027
  • Corpus Christi: Thursday 27 May 2027

The regional bus operator SIGA Rodoeste lists the same three religious dates in its holiday timetable calendar for 2026 to 2027.

Madeira's three regional holidays

Autonomy Day, 2 April. The newest of the three, created by Regional Legislative Decree 17/2024/M, which makes 2 April the Autonomy Day holiday in the Autonomous Region of Madeira. In 2027 it falls on the Friday after Easter.

Madeira Day, 1 July. Regional Decree 27/79/M made 1 July the holiday of the Autonomous Region of Madeira, and Regional Legislative Decree 1/89/M gave it its full name, the Day of the Autonomous Region of Madeira and of the Madeiran Communities. It honours both the region and Madeirans living abroad. In 2027 it is a Thursday.

26 December. Regional Legislative Decree 18/2002/M makes 26 December a holiday in the Autonomous Region of Madeira. In 2027 it falls on a Sunday, the day after Christmas, so the island has two holiday days back to back over that weekend, during the Christmas season in Funchal.

All three apply across the region, which under its statute includes Madeira, Porto Santo, the Desertas, the Selvagens and their islets.

Municipal holidays

Each municipality also marks a local holiday. Shops, offices and services in that municipality may close; check neighbouring municipalities separately. These are the dates we could confirm on official municipal pages:

MunicipalityDate in 2027WeekdayOccasion
Funchal21 AugustSaturdayFunchal City Day (Dia da Cidade do Funchal)
Santana25 MayTuesdayMunicipal holiday
Calheta24 JuneThursdaySão João (St John)
Câmara de Lobos4 OctoberMondayMunicipality Day (Dia do Concelho)

Porto Santo marks its Municipality Day (Dia do Concelho) on 24 June, the feast of São João; the municipal page we read describes the celebrations but does not itself use the word holiday. For Santa Cruz, the municipality that is home to Madeira Airport, and for Machico, we could not confirm a 2027 date on an official page, so check locally. In 2027 Funchal's holiday falls on a Saturday, the day before the Madeira Wine Festival, which runs from 22 August to 12 September 2027 in the official calendar.

Carnival is not a statutory holiday

Carnival Tuesday, 9 February in 2027, is not on the national list. Under article 235 of the Labour Code it can be observed as a holiday through a collective agreement or an employment contract, along with the municipal holiday. In practice the regional government has given its own staff time off (tolerância de ponto) on Carnival Tuesday and the following Wednesday morning in 2025 and in 2026, while keeping essential services running. We did not find a decision for 2027 when checking in November 2026. The Madeira Carnival itself runs in Funchal from 3 to 14 February 2027.

What changes on a public holiday

We have only described what the official sources say. Ask your hotel or the business itself about a specific day.

  • Buses. SIGA Rodoeste runs its Sunday timetable on public holidays, and lists the 2027 national and regional dates and 21 August in its holiday calendar. It also states that there are no trips on 25 December 2026. Check each operator's own timetable; our getting around guide and transport page explain who runs which routes.
  • The market. Funchal's municipal tourism listing for the Mercado dos Lavradores gives it as closed on Sundays and public holidays.
  • Restaurants and cafés. Under Portuguese rules, restaurants and drinks establishments set their own opening hours, although a municipality can impose restrictions. Many open on holidays; some close.
  • Other businesses. As Portugal's Constitutional Court has described the Labour Code, a holiday requires the closure or suspension of activities that are not permitted on Sundays. Activities allowed on a Sunday can carry on.
  • Walking trails. Holidays do not change the trail rules: each IFCN-managed classified trail covered by the system still needs a booking on the Simplifica portal, and IFCN's trail-status page is still the place to check. Our trail fees guide has the details.

Emergency services work every day of the year: the number is 112, and our emergency contacts page lists the others.

Holidays and events worth planning around

Several holidays coincide with the island's biggest events, which means fuller hotels and busier roads:

  • Easter, 26 to 28 March, and Autonomy Day, 2 April: two holiday Fridays in a row.
  • 1 May: the Flower Festival runs from 29 April to 30 May 2027, with the Great Allegoric Flower Parades listed for 2 and 16 May.
  • Corpus Christi, 27 May, and Portugal Day, 10 June: both on Thursdays. Portugal Day falls during the Atlantic Festival, listed for 4 to 27 June 2027.
  • 15 August: the Feast of Our Lady of Monte, celebrated by Funchal as its patron saint, with the main festivities at Monte on 14 and 15 August. The Monte cable car is the easy way up.
  • 31 December into 1 January: the New Year fireworks over Funchal bay. See our New Year fireworks guide.

For more on how the seasons and the festival calendar fit together, read our best time to visit guide and Madeira in winter, or browse all events. Practical tips for your stay are on the local tips page.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many public holidays does Madeira have in 2027?

Sixteen across the region: Portugal's 13 national holidays and three regional holidays (2 April, 1 July and 26 December). Each municipality adds one local holiday, such as 21 August in Funchal.

When is Easter in Madeira in 2027?

Good Friday is 26 March and Easter Sunday is 28 March 2027. Both are public holidays. Easter Monday is not a holiday in Portugal.

What is Madeira Day?

1 July, the Day of the Autonomous Region of Madeira and of the Madeiran Communities, a regional holiday set by regional decree. In 2027 it falls on a Thursday.

Is 26 December a holiday in Madeira?

Yes. Regional Legislative Decree 18/2002/M makes 26 December a holiday across the region, including Porto Santo. On mainland Portugal it is not a national holiday. In 2027 it falls on a Sunday.

Is Carnival Tuesday a holiday in Madeira?

Not by law. It is optional under the Labour Code, and in 2025 and 2026 the regional government gave its staff time off. In 2027 Carnival Tuesday is 9 February.

Are holidays moved to Monday when they fall at a weekend?

The Labour Code sets holidays by date, and the official 2027 bus holiday calendar lists them on their own dates, including the weekend ones such as 25 April, 1 May, 15 August and 21 August.

Do buses run on public holidays?

SIGA Rodoeste runs its Sunday timetable on public holidays and has announced no trips on 25 December 2026. Check the timetable of the operator you plan to use.

Is the Mercado dos Lavradores open on public holidays?

Funchal's municipal tourism listing gives the market as closed on Sundays and public holidays. Visit on a weekday or Saturday instead.
guides.bestTime: Book early for Easter (26 to 28 March 2027), the Flower Festival weekends in May and the New Year
guides.budget: Holiday weekends that coincide with festivals push up demand for rooms, hire cars and the Porto Santo crossing

guides.title: Madeira Trail Fees and Tourist Tax: What Visitors Pay
guides.summary: What Madeira charges visitors as of November 2026: trail fees from €4.50, Cabo Girão at €5, IFCN parking rates and the €2-a-night tourist tax, with exemptions and what is still undecided.
guides.html:
Madeira has added several visitor charges in recent years, and they are easy to confuse: a fee for classified walking trails, an entry charge at one famous viewpoint, parking charges at some forest car parks, and a municipal tourist tax added to your accommodation bill. None of them is large on its own, but they add up over a walking holiday, and trail access requires an online booking, and Cabo Girão tickets can be bought online. This guide lists each charge as the official pages state it as of November 2026, says who is exempt, and flags what is still undecided. Rates change, so check the linked official source before you travel.

The charges at a glance

  • IFCN-managed classified walking trails covered by the system (PR): €4.50 per trail per person over 12 for non-residents; full PR1 €10.50; combined one-day, three-day and seven-day rates for several trails, PR1 excluded. Booking a time slot is compulsory for ordinary visitors, including fee-exempt visitors; statutory access exceptions apply.
  • Cabo Girão viewpoint: €5.00 per non-resident visitor over 12, paid through the SIMplifica portal; residents and visitors with reduced mobility or using wheelchairs are exempt.
  • IFCN car parks: hourly charges at the Pico do Areeiro viewpoint, at Queimadas and at other forest-park car parks run by the IFCN, with the first 30 minutes free.
  • Municipal tourist tax: €2 per night for up to seven nights in Funchal and on Porto Santo; several other municipalities charge their own.
  • Cruise passengers in Funchal: €2 per passenger in transit who disembarks at the port.

The classified-trail fee and booking

Since 1 January 2026 the regional forestry and nature institute, the IFCN, has run a combined booking and fee system for the classified walking routes it manages. These are the waymarked PR routes, many of them levada walks such as Levada das 25 Fontes and Levada do Caldeirão Verde. The legal basis is Portaria n.º 801/2025 of 10 December, amended by Portaria n.º 48/2026 of 13 February.

Rates for visitors without an operator protocol, as of November 2026:

  • Single trail, except PR1: €4.50.
  • PR1 Vereda do Areeiro, only to the Pedra Rija viewpoint and back: €4.50.
  • Published full-PR1 tariff, including PR1.1 and PR1.2, with PR1.3 included when reopened: €10.50. A published tariff does not mean a closed trail is accessible.
  • Two or more trails in one day, excluding PR1: €9.00.
  • Two or more trails within three days, excluding PR1: €22.50.
  • Two or more trails within seven days, excluding PR1: €52.50.

The day and multi-day rates are discounts, not passes. You still book each trail, date and slot, and the portal applies the cheapest combination automatically at checkout. There is no separate button to buy a multi-day rate.

Who pays and who is exempt

The fee applies to non-residents. Exempt from paying, but still required to register and book: residents of the Autonomous Region of Madeira who prove it with a resident card and citizen card, children aged 12 or under, and people with a disability of 60% or more together with one accompanying guardian, on proof. Landowners crossing their own property and people providing essential public services are outside the system entirely.

How to book and pay

Booking is only online, on SIMplifica, the regional government's digital services portal. The IFCN does not take bookings or payments at its offices. Same-day and next-day bookings are possible while places remain. The tourism board recommends paying before you set off because mobile coverage in the mountains can be limited. Technical or card problems go to the SIMplifica contact centre.

Refunds and fines

You can ask the IFCN to reschedule or refund only if the trail was officially closed or restricted on your booking date, within 10 working days from the booking date, as the IFCN FAQ states. Rain, illness, a cancelled flight or a change of plan all forfeit the fee. Entering a PR without a booking is an infraction that can lead to a fine, the tourism board says; it does not state the amount, and we could not find it on an official page. Walking a trail that is officially closed is a separate offence under the regional trails law, with fines from €250 to €2,500 for an individual.

Trail status changes often. On the IFCN status table read on 16 November 2026, PR1 from Pico do Arieiro was listed as closed, while the PR1.2 route up Pico Ruivo from Achada do Teixeira was open. PR1.1 was open, and PR1.3 remained closed between Boca das Torrinhas and Encumeada. PR6 (25 Fontes), PR8 (Ponta de São Lourenço), PR9 (Caldeirão Verde) and PR11 (Balcões) were listed open; PR6 requires the one-way outward route and the bypass for the return. The official pages conflict on PR1: the status table labels it closed, and the live IFCN notice lists both its full route and Pedra Rija section as closed, while SIMplifica still lists tickets for both. The notice also lists PR1.3 as closed, so do not assume its northern section is accessible. When authorised to operate, it is two-way only as far as Pedra Rija, then one-way towards Pico Ruivo. Confirm current access with IFCN before booking or walking; a ticket listing is not proof that a route is open. Do not enter a closed route. The same IFCN notice says the forest road from Eira do Serrado to Pico do Areeiro remains closed. Check the IFCN status table and notices again on the day. Our levada walks guide covers status, distances and safety in detail.

Cabo Girão viewpoint

The glass-floored platform at Cabo Girão, above Câmara de Lobos, has an entry charge. The official SIMplifica portal states €5.00 for non-resident visitors over 12, with children 12 and under exempt, paid through the SIMplifica portal, as of November 2026. Residents with a valid SIMplifica resident card, and people with reduced mobility or using wheelchairs, are also exempt. The official portal lists daily opening from 08:00 to 20:00 as of November 2026; check its closure notices before travelling. Pay before you arrive, and keep the confirmation on your phone.

Parking at IFCN viewpoints and forest parks

As of November 2026, the IFCN's price list, in the same Portaria, sets hourly parking charges at car parks serving the parks and forest areas it manages directly:

  • Pico do Areeiro viewpoint: €4.00 per hour in 2026, first 30 minutes free, daily maximum €20.
  • Queimadas (the start of the Caldeirão Verde walk in Queimadas Forest Park): €2.00 per hour, first 30 minutes free, daily maximum €10.
  • Other IFCN car parks: €2.00 per hour, first 30 minutes free, daily maximum €5.

The same list shows higher rates scheduled for 2027 to 2029. The price list does not name the other car parks. At Queimadas, IFCN says parking can be paid at the reception centre. A long walk from Pico do Areeiro can reach the daily cap, which is one reason many walkers use a tour or taxi for linear routes.

Other IFCN prices as of November 2026: the Madeira Botanical Garden lists €10 for visitors over 12 in 2026, and the Portaria also prices the Casa das Tradições Madeirenses at Queimadas and the Ribeiro Frio aquaculture centre at €3 each for non-resident visitors over 12. Residents are exempt from several of these.

Other viewpoints and natural sites

We found no general entry charge on official pages for other well-known viewpoints, such as the Eira do Serrado viewpoint or the Balcões viewpoint. Balcões is reached on the PR11 trail, so the trail fee and booking apply there. The Ponta de São Lourenço walk is PR8, also covered by the trail fee. Divers should note that the IFCN Portaria sets a daily charge for diving in the Garajau, Desertas and Selvagens reserves for non-residents; ask your dive centre how the charge is handled.

The municipal tourist tax

Madeira has no single regional tourist tax. Each municipality decides its own, and the hotel or holiday let collects it and passes it on.

Funchal

The Funchal tax has applied since 1 October 2024. The municipality states it is €2 per night, up to a maximum of seven nights; nights after the seventh are not charged. It applies in hotels, quintas, country houses and local accommodation (holiday lets). Exemptions, with proof: residents of the Autonomous Region of Madeira, guests aged 12 or under, and guests with a certified disability of 60% or more.

Since 1 January 2025 Funchal has also charged €2 per cruise passenger in transit who disembarks at the port, with exemptions including children up to 12 and passengers whose final destination is Funchal, who pay the overnight tax instead.

The municipal page read as of November 2026 states €2. We could not confirm a subsequent rate or effective date from an official page, so check with your accommodation before budgeting for a future stay.

Porto Santo

On Porto Santo the municipal regulation sets €2 per paid night, per person, up to seven consecutive nights per stay (at most €14). It applies to guests aged 13 and over regardless of nationality or residence, so Madeira residents also pay here. Exemptions include stays for medical treatment (with one companion), people with a disability of 60% or more (with one companion), and children under 13. A break in the stay restarts the seven-night count.

The municipal practical guide read as of November 2026 states €2. We could not confirm a subsequent rate or effective date from an official page, so check with your accommodation before a future stay.

Other municipalities

Several other municipalities on Madeira island also charge a tourist tax under their own regulations, and the rates, caps and exemptions are not identical. We do not list rates for them here. Ask your accommodation when you book whether a tax applies and how it is paid. Our where to stay guide compares the main bases, including Caniço, Calheta and Machico.

How much to budget

For a week in Funchal with four €4.50 IFCN-covered trails, excluding PR1, booked on separate days, a non-resident adult without an exemption would pay €14 in tourist tax (seven nights at €2) and €18 in trail fees (four trails at €4.50), plus €5 if you visit Cabo Girão and any parking. For trails excluding PR1, two single trails on the same day cost the same as the €9 day rate, so the saving only appears with three or more trails in a day (€9 instead of €13.50) or enough trails inside a three-day or seven-day window to exceed those rates. These examples use rates as of November 2026. Use these sums as a guide only and check current rates before you go. For the bigger cost picture, see our first-timer's guide and the local tips page.

What stays free

Beaches and lidos have their own rules, so check access arrangements for bathing spots such as Praia Formosa; municipal lidos set their own prices. Town centres are free to explore; churches and markets such as the Mercado dos Lavradores have their own visiting arrangements. Unclassified paths are not covered by the trail fee, but the IFCN does not maintain or recommend them, so the saving is not worth the risk on an unknown route.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the hiking fee in Madeira?

As of November 2026, non-residents over 12 pay €4.50 per IFCN-covered trail except PR1, a published €10.50 tariff for the full PR1 Vereda do Areeiro, usable only when that route is open, or €9.00 for two or more trails in one day excluding PR1. You must also book an entry slot on the SIMplifica portal.

Do children pay the trail fee or tourist tax?

Children aged 12 or under do not pay the trail fee but still need a booking. In Funchal, guests aged 12 or under are exempt from the tourist tax; on Porto Santo, children under 13 are exempt.

Is there a tourist tax in Madeira?

Yes, at municipal level. Funchal and Porto Santo charge €2 per night for up to seven nights as of November 2026, and other municipalities have their own rules. Check with your accommodation for any subsequent change before a future stay.

Do I have to pay to visit Cabo Girão?

Yes. The official SIMplifica portal lists €5.00 for non-resident visitors over 12, with children 12 and under exempt, paid through the SIMplifica portal.

Can I pay the trail fee at the trailhead?

No. Booking and payment are online only, through SIMplifica. Mobile coverage is weak in the mountains, so book before you set out.

Do Madeira residents pay these charges?

Residents are exempt from the trail fee with proof but must still book. They are exempt from Funchal's tourist tax, but not from Porto Santo's.

guides.title: Porto Santo Travel Guide: Ferry, Flights, Beach and Walks
guides.summary: Porto Santo is Madeira’s small, dry, sandy neighbour, 71 km away. How to get there by ferry or plane, what to do on the island, and whether a day trip or a few nights suits you, as of November 2026.
guides.html:
Porto Santo is the second inhabited island of the Madeira archipelago and the opposite of Madeira in almost every way. Where Madeira is steep, green and rocky, Porto Santo is low, dry and golden, with a beach that runs along its whole south coast. Porto Santo Line puts it 71 km from Madeira. Visit Madeira describes it as the smallest inhabited island of the archipelago, and UNESCO has listed the island and its surrounding sea as a biosphere reserve since 2020. People from Madeira go there in summer for the sand; visitors from abroad usually add it as a day trip or a two or three night break.

Getting there by ferry: the Lobo Marinho

As of November 2026, the ferry is run by Porto Santo Line, and its ship is the Lobo Marinho. It sails between the port of Funchal and the harbour beside Vila Baleira, carries passengers and cars, and has a sun deck, a cinema room, a bar lounge and a restaurant. The company's FAQ gives the crossing as about 2 hours 15 minutes and the ship's capacity as 1,153 passengers and 145 cars. Foot passengers must be at the terminal at least 30 minutes before departure; drivers must be at the car deck an hour before.

Timetable patterns

The timetable changes month by month, so read the dated table on the operator's site for your dates. As published in November 2026:

  • August 2026 had a sailing every day: out from Funchal at 08:00, with a second round trip on several days a week. Most days had a 20:00 return; on 7, 14, 20 and 28 August the returns were at 12:00 and 22:30.
  • December 2026 mostly runs out at 08:00 and back at 18:00 (19:00 on Sundays), with no sailing on 2, 9, 15, 22, 25 and 29 December. On 4 December the return leaves at 16:00. On 24 December the return leaves at 12:00, and on 31 December at 11:30, so New Year's Eve leaves very little time ashore for a day trip.
  • For January 2027, check the operator directly: we could not retrieve a timetable for that month. The company states that its timetable might be changed.

On dates with an 08:00 outward sailing and an 18:00 return, the roughly 2-hour-15-minute crossing leaves about seven hours ashore before allowing for boarding. Shorter return schedules leave much less time. If the forecast is rough, ask the company whether the sailing is going ahead before you leave for the port.

Ferry fares, as of November 2026

Porto Santo Line's 2026 price list has two seasons (April to September, and January to March plus October to December) and separate prices for Madeira residents who receive the Social Mobility Allowance. Visitors pay the prices without that allowance. For tourist class, as of November 2026:

Ticket (visitor fare)April to SeptemberJanuary to March, October to December
Adult return€72.02€58.90
Adult one way€43.83€37.12
Child 5 to 11, return€36.00€29.44
Car up to 7 seats, return€250.40€195.74

Children under 5 travel free but need a ticket. A monthly fuel surcharge is added to these prices, and first class costs more. The operator also sells a One Day Cruise (out and back the same day) from the same base fare, with optional transfers, a bike, an island tour, golf or a jeep tour added; as of November 2026, the golf version with transfers in Funchal or Caniço and Porto Santo was €107.10 in the low season, before the fuel surcharge. Our Porto Santo day trip page compares the options.

If you hire a car on Madeira and want to take it across, check first that the rental agreement allows the crossing and that the insurance covers Porto Santo.

Getting there by plane

As of November 2026, Binter flies between Madeira Airport and Porto Santo Airport. Its Madeira to Porto Santo page describes daily morning and afternoon flights, with the islands about 25 minutes apart. Visit Madeira also notes that Porto Santo is an hour and a half's flight from Lisbon. Flying makes sense if you are short of time or prone to seasickness; the ferry is useful if you want a car or a sea crossing as part of the day. Prices vary by date, so compare both for your trip. See getting around Madeira and the transportation page for buses to the port and the airport.

The beach

The reason most people go is the beach. Visit Madeira describes it as stretching for 9 km along the entire south coast of the island, with warm, clear water and, on most days, somewhere the sea is calm. It also mentions that swell close to shore can make entry harder for less confident swimmers on some days. The tourism board speaks of the island's therapeutic sands; we cannot verify health claims, but the sand itself is soft and golden, unlike almost anything on Madeira.

Our page for Porto Santo beach covers the main stretch. At the south-west tip, Ponta da Calheta is quieter and more rugged, with parking, changing rooms, toilets and a restaurant, and a view of Ilhéu da Cal (also called Ilhéu de Baixo), an islet whose old lime mines can still be seen in the cliffs. For how this compares with the bathing places on the main island, read the best beaches and pools in Madeira.

Vila Baleira and Casa Colombo

Vila Baleira is the island's main town, with cafés, shops and services behind the beach. Explore the centre on foot.

The main sight is Casa Colombo, the Columbus House Museum on Travessa da Sacristia. Visit Madeira says the building is said to have been the home of Christopher Columbus, who lived for a time in the archipelago and married Filipa Moniz. The museum covers Columbus and Porto Santo's history. The Regional Culture Directorate gives the following hours, as of November 2026: Monday to Friday 10:00 to 12:30 and 14:00 to 17:30; Saturday 10:00 to 13:00; closed Sundays and public holidays. Its schedule differs from the tourism board's page, so reconfirm before travelling.

In September the island holds the Columbus Festival; Visit Madeira gives the 2027 dates as 23 to 26 September, with street theatre, concerts and a recreated 16th-century market.

Viewpoints and walks

Porto Santo's interior is a ring of low volcanic peaks with wide views over the beach and the sea. The regional nature institute IFCN manages three classified walking routes on the island. Their status checked in November 2026:

  • PS PR1, Vereda do Pico Branco e Terra Chã: 2.7 km each way, from the ER 111 road over Pico Branco to Terra Chã on the north coast. Open.
  • PS PR2, Vereda do Pico do Castelo: 3.2 km or 4.6 km, from Moledo to Pico do Castelo. Open.
  • PS PR3, Levada do Pico Castelo: 4.1 km, Camacha to Capela da Graça. Closed.

Trail status changes, so check the IFCN trail-status page on the day. For these IFCN-managed classified trails, the individual visitor fee is €4.50 per route, as of November 2026. Book and pay online through SIMplifica before starting. Madeira residents, children aged 12 or under, and people with a documented disability of at least 60% with one accompanying legal guardian are exempt from payment but still need registration/booking; our trail fees guide explains how it works and how to check whether a route needs a slot on the SIMplifica portal. The routes here are shorter and lower than the big walks on Madeira, such as the Pico do Arieiro to Pico Ruivo hike, but they are exposed: take water, a hat and sun cream.

For views without a walk, the Portela viewpoint above Vila Baleira looks along the whole beach (it is also one of the island's two launch posts for the New Year fireworks). Ponta da Calheta at the far end of the beach is a good place to watch the sunset.

Golf

Porto Santo has an 18-hole course designed by Severiano Ballesteros, which Visit Madeira says opened in October 2004, plus a separate 9-hole par 3 course. Check course conditions with the club before travelling. Green fees are set by the club, so ask it directly; Porto Santo Line's golf day package is one way to combine the crossing and a round. See golf in Madeira for the courses on the main island.

When to go

Porto Santo is drier than Funchal and a little cooler at the height of the day. IPMA's 1991 to 2020 normals for the Porto Santo station give 381.7 mm of rain a year, against 574.3 mm at the Funchal Observatory, with a mean daily maximum of 25.7°C in August and 18.4°C in January.

  • July to September is beach season, when the island is at its busiest with visitors from Madeira and the ferry runs every day. Book accommodation and car places on the ferry early for August.
  • May, June and October are quieter and still warm enough for the beach on calm days.
  • November to March is very quiet. The ferry does not sail every day, and the beach is for walking more than swimming. It suits walkers, golfers and anyone who wants empty space.

Compare the seasons on both islands in the best time to visit Madeira and the Madeira weather page.

Day trip or stay?

A day trip works if you mainly want the beach, a walk through Vila Baleira and lunch. On dates with an 08:00 outward sailing and an 18:00 return, you get roughly seven hours ashore before boarding; other schedules differ. Remember that the crossing adds about four and a half hours of sailing to your day.

Two or three nights make more sense if you want to walk the PR routes, play golf, see the island's sunsets or simply slow down. Evenings in Vila Baleira are quiet, and you are not watching the clock for the last ferry. Porto Santo Line sells ferry and hotel packages, and the island has a range of hotels and apartments along the beach.

A typical stay on Madeira can absorb either. The 10-day itinerary has room for an overnight on Porto Santo, while a shorter trip such as the 7-day itinerary can swap one day for a ferry day trip. If you are deciding where to base yourself, see where to stay in Madeira.

Practical notes

  • Porto Santo uses the same currency, time zone and emergency number (112) as Madeira; see emergency contacts.
  • Shade is scarce on the beach and the walks. The sun is strong even when the breeze feels cool.
  • For food, look for fresh fish and Madeiran staples such as bolo do caco and grilled limpets.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long is the ferry from Madeira to Porto Santo?

Porto Santo Line gives the crossing on the Lobo Marinho as about 2 hours 15 minutes each way, between Funchal and Vila Baleira.

How much is the ferry to Porto Santo?

As of November 2026, a visitor's adult return in tourist class costs €72.02 from April to September and €58.90 from January to March and October to December, plus a monthly fuel surcharge. Children under 5 travel free with a ticket.

Can you fly from Madeira to Porto Santo?

Yes. As of November 2026, Binter flies between Madeira Airport and Porto Santo Airport, and describes daily morning and afternoon flights about 25 minutes long.

Is Porto Santo worth a day trip?

Yes, if you want a sandy beach, which Madeira itself mostly lacks. With an 08:00 outward sailing and an 18:00 return, you have about seven hours ashore before boarding; check your exact date. Stay a night or two if you also want the walks, golf or a sunset at Ponta da Calheta.

Does the ferry to Porto Santo run every day?

Not all year. As published in November 2026, the August 2026 timetable had a sailing every day, while December 2026 has several days without a sailing, including Christmas Day. Always check the dated timetable for your month.

guides.title: Things to Do in Madeira: A Guide by Interest
guides.summary: Things to do in Madeira by interest: Funchal's old town and market, Monte by cable car, the high peaks, levada walks, north-coast lava pools, whale watching and Porto Santo's sand.
guides.html:
Madeira rewards travellers who pick a theme for each day. The island is steep and the roads wind, so a morning in Funchal, an afternoon on a levada and an evening on the north coast is more driving than holiday. This guide sorts the best things to do by interest, from the capital's markets to the lava pools of the north coast and the long sandy beach on Porto Santo. Every item links to its own page with practical details. Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal, so you pay in euros, and the emergency number is 112.

Funchal: the capital on foot

Funchal is a useful starting point, and its centre is compact enough to walk. Start early at the Mercado dos Lavradores, the covered farmers' market, where tropical fruit is stacked under the tiled entrance and the fish hall sells black scabbardfish caught in deep water off the island. Walk east into the old town (Zona Velha), where the painted doors of Rua de Santa Maria turn a narrow street into an open-air gallery, and evenings fill the restaurant terraces.

In the centre, the Sé, Funchal's cathedral, is worth a look inside for its carved and gilded woodwork. A few streets away, Blandy's Wine Lodge runs tours and tastings in its old lodge, and football fans head to the harbour for the CR7 Museum, dedicated to Cristiano Ronaldo. The seafront promenade links all of this and continues west toward the hotel zone.

Gardens and cable cars

A classic half day in Madeira starts at the seafront station of the Monte cable car, which lifts you over the rooftops of Funchal to the hillside parish of Monte. At the top, the Monte Palace Tropical Garden mixes exotic planting, lakes and art collections on a steep hillside. Then comes the classic way down: the Monte toboggan ride, wicker sledges (carros de cesto) pushed and steered by drivers down the steep road from Monte.

A second cable car runs between Monte and the Madeira Botanical Garden, whose terraces of native and imported plants look down over the bay. East of the city, the Palheiro Gardens are quieter, with formal beds and camellias around an old estate. If you visit in spring, the Madeira Flower Festival fills Funchal with floral carpets and a parade.

Peaks and viewpoints

The mountains in the middle of the island are the reason many people come. Pico do Areeiro, reached by road, is the third-highest point on Madeira at 1,818 metres, and at dawn it often sits above a sea of cloud. Pico Ruivo, at 1,862 metres, is the highest point of the archipelago. The famous ridge path between the two, the PR1 Vereda do Areeiro, was listed as closed as of November 2026. The current IFCN notice explicitly lists both the full route and the section to the Pedra Rija viewpoint as closed, so do not enter either section. Pico Ruivo itself can still be reached on the shorter PR1.2 from Achada do Teixeira, which was listed as open. Check the IFCN trail-status page and current notices on the day you go. The Poiso road service was suspended when checked in November 2026, and IFCN also reported the Eira do Serrado forest road closed, so confirm road access before driving up. As of November 2026, the published IFCN parking tariff at Pico do Areeiro is €4 per hour, with the first 30 minutes free and a €20 daily maximum; parking and trail fees are separate.

Lower down, the Eira do Serrado viewpoint looks straight down into the village of Curral das Freiras, ringed by mountains. On the south coast west of Funchal, the glass-floored platform of the Cabo Girão Skywalk lets you look straight down a sheer sea cliff to the terraced fields at its foot. As of November 2026, adult entry is €5; children aged 12 or under, Madeira residents and people with reduced mobility or using wheelchairs are exempt. Buy through SIMplifica and check access notices and parking arrangements before travelling. For forest views, the short walk to the Balcões viewpoint at Ribeiro Frio (PR11) looks over the laurel-covered valleys toward the peaks.

Levada walks

Levadas are the irrigation channels that carry water from the wet north and the mountains to farmland in the south, and the maintenance paths beside them form walking routes that vary in difficulty and can include narrow paths, tunnels and exposed drops. The levada walks overview explains how they work and what to bring. Two classics:

  • Levada das 25 Fontes (PR6) from Rabaçal, open as of November 2026 with one-way circulation: out along the levada, back by an alternative path.
  • Levada do Caldeirão Verde (PR9) from the Queimadas Forest Park near Santana, through tunnels to a waterfall pool, also open as of November 2026.

Both run through the Laurisilva, the laurel forest that has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1999. Under the 2026 system, visitors must book a time slot and pay online before starting classified trails managed by IFCN. As of November 2026, the individual fee is €4.50 per route, except the full PR1 tariff of €10.50 when that route is open. Madeira residents, children aged 12 or under, and people with a documented disability of at least 60% with one accompanying legal guardian are exempt from payment but still register/book. Use the SIMplifica portal; further amounts and rules are in our trail fees and tourist tax guide, and the walking side of the island is covered in the levada walks guide. Hikers who want a full week on foot can follow the 7-day hiking itinerary.

At the eastern tip, Ponta de São Lourenço (PR8) is a different landscape: bare, wind-scoured volcanic ridges with sea on both sides. It was listed as open in November 2026. On the high plateau in the west, the old laurels of Fanal stand in a meadow that is often wrapped in mist; the PR13 trail to it was closed at the same date. Check road access separately before driving to the forest.

The north coast and lava pools

The north side of Madeira is greener, wetter and wilder. At Porto Moniz, the natural pools are basins of black lava rock filled by the Atlantic, with steps and ladders for swimming. A short drive east, Seixal has the Seixal natural pools and the dark sand of Seixal beach, framed by green cliffs.

In Santana, the traditional thatched houses are small A-framed buildings painted red, white and blue. At the far west, the Achadas da Cruz cable car drops down a sheer cliff to fields on a fajã (a strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff); check it is running before you drive out. The São Vicente Caves, lava tubes open to the public since 1996, were marked CLOSED on the tourism board's page in November 2026, so do not plan a day around them.

The sea

Madeira's coast drops steeply into deep water, which brings whales and dolphins close to shore. Whale and dolphin watching trips leave from marinas along the south coast. Divers and snorkellers head for the Garajau Marine Reserve below Caniço, where scuba diving centres run guided dives and the pebble Praia do Garajau sits under the cliffs.

A full-day boat trip to the Desertas Islands crosses to the uninhabited islands of the Desertas nature reserve. For swimming close to Funchal, the Lido bathing complex has seawater pools and sea access, and Praia Formosa is the city's long pebble beach. Adrenaline options include canyoning in the ravines, paragliding above the south-west coast and surfing on the north and west swells. Our beaches and pools guide compares every swimming spot.

Food and wine

Madeiran food is built around the grill and the sea. Order espetada, beef skewered on bay-laurel sticks, with bolo do caco flatbread spread with garlic butter. Grilled limpets (lapas grelhadas) arrive sizzling in their pan, and espada com banana pairs black scabbardfish with banana. Fried maize cubes, milho frito, come on the side.

Câmara de Lobos, the fishing town just west of Funchal, is the place to try poncha, the island's drink of aguardente, honey and lemon. For the fortified wine, book a Madeira wine tasting, and if you are here in late summer the Madeira Wine Festival celebrates the harvest. Finish with a slice of bolo de mel, the dark sugar-cane honey cake.

Porto Santo

Porto Santo is the archipelago's second inhabited island and its opposite: low, dry and fringed by sand. The headline is Porto Santo beach, a 9-kilometre stretch of golden sand with calm water, and at its western end Ponta da Calheta looks out to rocky islets. In Vila Baleira, the Casa Colombo museum tells the story of Christopher Columbus's time on the island.

You can get there by the Lobo Marinho ferry from Funchal or by a short flight to Porto Santo airport; see the Porto Santo day trip page and the full Porto Santo travel guide. In November 2026 the operator's published timetable showed an 08:00 departure from Funchal on most days and no sailing on some days, so check the month you travel.

With children

Children tend to love the cable car and the toboggan ride down from Monte, and the pools at the Lido and Porto Moniz are alternatives to open shingle beaches, subject to sea conditions, supervision and any closures. The Madeira Whale Museum in Caniçal, near Machico, explains the island's whaling past and the marine life around it. Short, wide levadas such as the PR9.1 accessible section at Queimadas suit small legs better than the longer classics. Under-13s are exempt from the trail fee but still need a booking.

On a rainy day

When cloud sits on the mountains, stay low and south. Funchal's indoor options cover a full day: the market, Blandy's, the cathedral and the CR7 Museum, followed by lunch in the old town. The Whale Museum is a good covered morning, and the south coast is often drier than the north even when the peaks are hidden. Check our weather page before choosing which side of the island to visit, and keep mountain walks for a clear day.

Quick planning notes

  • Where to base yourself: Funchal for first visits; see where to stay in Madeira.
  • Getting around: a hire car reaches the north coast and trailheads; buses link the towns. See getting around Madeira.
  • How long: the 5-day and 7-day itineraries cover the highlights.
  • First trip: read the first-timer's guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the one thing not to miss in Madeira?

For most visitors it is the mountains: a sunrise or clear morning at Pico do Areeiro, followed by a levada walk in the laurel forest. If you only have time in Funchal, take the cable car to Monte and ride the toboggan down.

Can you walk from Pico do Areeiro to Pico Ruivo right now?

No. As of November 2026, IFCN listed both the full PR1 and the section from Pico do Areeiro to the Pedra Rija viewpoint as closed. Pico Ruivo was reachable on PR1.2 from Achada do Teixeira. Check the IFCN trail-status page on the day.

Do I need to book levada walks in advance?

Yes, for classified trails managed by IFCN. Visitors book an entry time slot and pay the fee on the SIMplifica portal; bookings for the same or next day are possible when slots remain. Residents and children aged 12 or under do not pay but still register.

Is Madeira good for a beach holiday?

Madeira itself has mostly pebble and rock beaches, lidos and lava pools rather than long sand. For a sandy beach, add a few days on Porto Santo, whose main beach runs for about 9 kilometres.

Are the São Vicente Caves open?

The tourism board's page showed them as closed in November 2026. Check again before your trip, and plan the north coast around Porto Moniz, Seixal and Santana instead.

Pick a few themes, give each its own day, and leave a spare day for the weather: in Madeira the best plan is the one that moves with the clouds.
guides.bestTime: April to October for walking and swimming; winter for mild city days
guides.budget: Moderate: many viewpoints and walks cost little beyond trail fees, while tours, boat trips and cable cars add up

guides.title: Where to Stay in Madeira: Best Areas by Traveller Type
guides.summary: Compare Madeira's bases: Funchal centre and Lido, Caniço, Câmara de Lobos, the sunny south-west, the green north coast, Santana, Machico and Porto Santo, with weather and transfer trade-offs.
guides.html:
Where you sleep in Madeira decides how much of your holiday you spend in a car. The island's mountainous centre means that two places that look close on a map can be a long, slow drive apart, and the weather on the north coast can be grey while Funchal is in sunshine. Most first-time visitors are best served by a base on the south coast, but walkers, families and travellers chasing quiet all have good reasons to look elsewhere. This guide goes area by area, from central Funchal to Porto Santo, and explains who each one suits.

The weather trade-off

Madeira has distinct microclimates. The tourism board puts it simply: the south is usually warmer and drier, while the north and the mountains are more exposed to wind and rain. In practice, a south-coast base gives you more sunny evenings on the terrace, while a north-coast base puts you closer to the laurel forest and the trailheads in exchange for more cloud and showers. Mist in the mountains can sit over the island while the coast is clear. Check our weather page for the season you are travelling in, and read the best time to visit Madeira if your dates are flexible.

Transfers from the airport

Madeira airport (FNC) is at Santa Cruz on the east coast, so Machico and Caniço are nearby options, Funchal is further west, and bases in the far west and on the north coast can mean longer transfers. The SIGA network's Aerobus service links the airport with Funchal, and a regional tourist ticket introduced in 2026 also covers it. For bases outside Funchal, a hire car or a pre-booked transfer is usually simpler than changing buses with luggage. Strong winds sometimes disrupt flights, so avoid a remote base for the first night if your plans are tight. See getting around Madeira for buses and driving.

Funchal centre and the old town

Central Funchal is the best choice for a first visit without a car. You can walk to the Mercado dos Lavradores, the cathedral, the marina and the seafront station of the Monte cable car, and buses to the rest of the island leave from the city. The old town (Zona Velha), at the eastern end of the centre, has a choice of restaurants and the painted doors of Rua de Santa Maria.

Suits: first-timers, couples, city-break travellers, anyone relying on buses. Trade-offs: streets climb steeply away from the sea, parking is limited and the old town can be lively at night. In December the city is the place to be for Christmas in Funchal and the New Year fireworks; book well ahead and read our fireworks guide.

The Lido hotel zone

West of the centre, the hotel zone around the Lido is where many of Funchal's larger resort hotels sit along the cliffs. It is quieter than the centre, and the Lido bathing complex with its seawater pools is on the doorstep. A seafront promenade continues west toward Praia Formosa, with Doca do Cavacas, a lava-rock bathing spot, between the Lido and Praia Formosa.

Suits: couples and families who want a pool-and-sea holiday with the city a bus ride or long walk away. Trade-offs: it feels more resort than town, and the walk back from the centre is uphill in places.

Caniço and Caniço de Baixo

Caniço, east of Funchal, divides into the town on the hill and Caniço de Baixo by the sea, where hotels and apartments line the cliffs above small bathing areas. The Garajau Marine Reserve and Praia do Garajau are nearby, which makes this a natural base for snorkelling and scuba diving.

Suits: divers, families, travellers who want short airport transfers and a calmer stay. Trade-offs: you will want a car or rely on buses to reach Funchal for dinner.

Câmara de Lobos

Just west of Funchal, Câmara de Lobos is a working fishing town with brightly painted boats in its small bay and bars known for poncha. It sits close to the Cabo Girão Skywalk and within easy reach of Funchal, so it works as a characterful alternative to the capital.

Suits: travellers who want local atmosphere and fish restaurants with Funchal nearby. Trade-offs: fewer accommodation options, and the town's tourist tax runs on its own rules.

Ponta do Sol and Calheta

The south-west coast is the sunny, slower side of Madeira. Ponta do Sol is a small town in a steep valley with a pebble beach and a seafront that catches the evening light. Further west, Calheta has a marina and the sheltered Calheta beach, with the cliff-foot villages of Jardim do Mar and Paul do Mar nearby, popular with surfers. From here the road climbs quickly to the Paul da Serra plateau and the Rabaçal trailhead for the Levada das 25 Fontes.

Suits: couples, remote workers, walkers who want western levadas and sunsets. Trade-offs: a car is close to essential, and Funchal and the airport are a long drive away.

The north coast: Porto Moniz, Seixal and São Vicente

The north is Madeira at its greenest. Porto Moniz is built around its lava-rock natural pools, and nearby Seixal has natural pools and a dark-sand beach. São Vicente, in the middle of the coast, is a good central point for exploring the north. The laurel forest of the Laurisilva and the old trees at Fanal are close by.

Suits: nature lovers, return visitors, travellers who prefer quiet evenings and do not mind cloud. Trade-offs: more rain and wind, fewer restaurants, and long drives to Funchal and the airport. Many people spend one or two nights here as part of a longer trip rather than a full week.

Santana

Santana, on the north-east coast, is known for its thatched A-frame houses and is a useful base for walkers aiming at the high peaks and the forest. The Queimadas Forest Park, the start of the Levada do Caldeirão Verde, is above the town, and Achada do Teixeira, the starting point of the shorter route up Pico Ruivo, is reached from here too.

Suits: hikers, rural-stay fans, travellers who like to be first on the trail. Trade-offs: quiet in the evening, cooler and wetter than the south coast, and best with a car. The 7-day hiking itinerary shows how a Santana base fits a walking week.

Machico

Machico, beside the airport on the east coast, has a sheltered bay with a golden-sand beach, and nearby Caniçal has the Madeira Whale Museum and the small Prainha do Caniçal. It is a base for exploring the east, including the walk out to Ponta de São Lourenço.

Suits: short stays, early or late flights, families who want a calm beach. Trade-offs: aircraft noise near the runway, and a drive or bus ride to Funchal's restaurants.

Porto Santo

Porto Santo is the island to choose for a beach holiday. Its main beach runs for about 9 kilometres of golden sand, and most accommodation sits along it or in Vila Baleira, the small main town. You reach it by the Lobo Marinho ferry from Funchal or by a short flight to Porto Santo airport; the ferry timetable varies by month, and in November 2026 some days had no sailing at all.

Suits: beach lovers, families with young children, a relaxing end to a walking trip. Trade-offs: a quieter stay outside summer, with the museum and golf as alternatives to the beach and island walks. Read the Porto Santo travel guide before booking.

How to choose

  • First visit, no car: central Funchal or the old town.
  • Pool and sea, close to the city: the Lido hotel zone.
  • Diving and a short transfer: Caniço de Baixo.
  • Sunsets and western levadas: Ponta do Sol or Calheta.
  • Hiking the peaks and forest: Santana, or a split with the north coast.
  • Sand: Porto Santo, at least for a few nights.

A popular split is four or five nights in Funchal followed by two nights on the north coast or in the south-west. Check the locally set nightly tourist tax for each base; our trail fees and tourist tax guide explains it. For a full planning checklist, read the first-timer's guide and things to do in Madeira.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best area to stay in Madeira for a first visit?

Central Funchal. You can walk to the market, old town, cathedral and Monte cable car, and the island's buses start from the city, so a car is optional for the first few days.

Is it better to stay on the north or the south coast?

For sunshine and restaurants, the south: it is usually warmer and drier. For forest walks, lava pools and quiet, the north. Many visitors split their stay between the two.

Where should I stay in Madeira without a car?

Funchal, either the centre, the old town or the Lido zone. SIGA buses and the Aerobus connect the city with the airport and much of the island, and tours cover the north.

Where should hikers stay in Madeira?

Santana puts you close to Queimadas, the Caldeirão Verde levada and the route to Pico Ruivo; the south-west suits the Rabaçal levadas. Book trail slots on the SIMplifica portal and check the IFCN trail-status page on the day.

Should I stay on Porto Santo or Madeira?

Madeira for walking, gardens and variety; Porto Santo for a long sandy beach. Adding two or three nights on Porto Santo to a Madeira trip gives you both.
