destinations.name: Calheta, Jardim do Mar and Paul do Mar
destinations.tagline: West-coast sand beach and marina, surf villages and the Rabaçal trails
destinations.summary: Calheta has a rare sand beach beside its marina, a contemporary art museum and a rum mill, with the surf villages of Jardim do Mar and Paul do Mar below the cliffs.
destinations.html:
Calheta is the largest municipality on Madeira's west coast, spreading over eight parishes from the sea to the Paul da Serra plateau. The town of Calheta sits by the coast around a recreational harbour and a 100-metre sand beach, one of the few sandy beaches on the main island. It suits families and couples who want a sunny base in the west with easy swimming.

Two smaller villages sit below the cliffs further west. Jardim do Mar is a favourite with surfers, thanks to a reliable swell and a pretty seafront of stone lanes. Paul do Mar, sheltered by tall cliffs, remains a working fishing village and is also known to surfers. Back in Calheta, the Engenho da Calheta, one of Madeira's old sugar cane mills, still makes rum and sugar cane honey, and the Casa das Mudas houses a contemporary art museum above the bay.

What to do

  • Swim at Calheta beach, then visit the Engenho da Calheta rum mill.
  • Watch or join the surfing at Jardim do Mar and Paul do Mar.
  • Walk the Levada das 25 Fontes from Rabaçal, inside the Madeira Natural Park.
  • Drive to Ponta do Pargo for the lighthouse and sunset views at the island's western tip.

Rabaçal, up on the Paul da Serra plateau, is the trailhead for some of the island's most popular levada walks through the laurel forest. As of November 2026 IFCN lists PR6 Levada das 25 Fontes open, with a one-way circuit: follow the levada out and return via the signed Bypass. These are classified trails: visitors book online in advance through SIMplifica and pay unless exempt, and routes can close after storms or fires, so read our trail fees guide and check the official trail status on the day. The marina is also a departure point for whale and dolphin trips.

The expressway along the west coast makes Calheta far easier to reach than it used to be, linking it with Ponta do Sol and the VR1 at Ribeira Brava for the run to Funchal and the airport. The old coastal road down to Jardim do Mar and Paul do Mar is still narrow and steep, so allow extra time for those villages.

destinations.name: Câmara de Lobos
destinations.tagline: Fishing town of painted boats, poncha bars and the Cabo Girão cliff
destinations.summary: Câmara de Lobos is a fishing town just west of Funchal: colourful boats in a small bay Churchill painted, poncha bars and the glass skywalk at Cabo Girão.
destinations.html:
Câmara de Lobos sits on the south coast a short drive west of Funchal, and it still earns its living partly from the sea. Brightly painted wooden fishing boats, called xavelhas, are pulled up on the slipway of a small, sheltered bay ringed by houses and cafes. The town has a strong claim to being where Madeira's settlement began: the regional tourism board records that João Gonçalves Zarco lived here from 1420 to 1424, before moving to Funchal.

The bay owes some of its fame to Winston Churchill. In January 1950 he set up his easel at the Espírito Santo viewpoint at the entrance to town and painted the harbour, and the spot now carries his name. The view has changed surprisingly little. Down on the waterfront, small bars serve poncha, the island's drink of sugar cane rum, honey and lemon, and the restaurants lean on fresh fish, espada and grilled limpets.

What to do

  • Walk the harbour and the old fishermen's quarter, then try a poncha where the locals drink it.
  • Stand on the glass platform of the Cabo Girão skywalk, 580 metres above the sea.
  • Drive up to the Eira do Serrado viewpoint and look down into Curral das Freiras (the Nuns' Valley).
  • Swim off the pebbles at Praia Formosa on the walk back towards Funchal.

The municipality reaches well inland. Curral das Freiras, its largest parish, lies at the bottom of a deep valley ringed by peaks; it takes its name from the nuns of Funchal's Santa Clara Convent, who fled there when pirates attacked the city in 1566. Higher villages such as Jardim da Serra and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos are farming country of terraces and vines.

Because it is so close to Funchal, most visitors come for an afternoon and evening rather than a stay, though a few small hotels make it a quieter alternative base. The VR1 expressway runs just above town, so the airport, the west coast and Ribeira Brava are all within easy reach.

destinations.name: Caniço and Caniço de Baixo
destinations.tagline: Quiet resort east of Funchal by the Garajau marine reserve and Cristo Rei
destinations.summary: Caniço and its seaside resort of Caniço de Baixo give you calm hotels, clear water for diving in the Garajau reserve and fast access to Funchal and the airport.
destinations.html:
Caniço lies on the south coast between Funchal and the airport, in the municipality of Santa Cruz. The old village centre sits up the slope around its church, while Caniço de Baixo, below it, is a low-rise resort of hotels and apartments built along the cliffs. It suits travellers who want a calmer base than the city, with the sea on the doorstep and Funchal a short drive away.

The coast here is protected. The Garajau marine reserve covers the water off the headland of Ponta do Garajau, and the regional tourism board describes it as one of the most sought-after dive sites in Madeira. Above it, the Cristo Rei statue, inaugurated on 30 October 1927, looks out over the reserve, Caniço de Baixo and part of Funchal bay.

What to do

  • Snorkel or scuba dive in the Garajau marine reserve.
  • Walk out to the Cristo Rei viewpoint and swim at the pebble cove of Praia do Garajau below it.
  • Take a boat trip to the Desertas Islands or go whale and dolphin watching along the south coast.
  • Spend an afternoon at the Palheiro Gardens, just inland on the way to Funchal.

Swimming here is mostly from rock platforms, ladders and small lidos rather than sand, so water shoes help. Sea conditions change with the swell, and the cliff paths are steep in places. Evenings are quiet: a few restaurants and hotel bars rather than nightlife.

Location is the main practical advantage. Madeira Airport is a few minutes east on the VR1 expressway, which also brings Funchal's restaurants and the Monte cable car within easy reach. Heading the other way, Machico and the walk at Ponta de São Lourenço make a straightforward half-day.

destinations.name: Funchal
destinations.tagline: Madeira's capital of gardens, cable cars, markets and a working harbour
destinations.summary: Funchal is the island's capital and best base: the farmers' market, the painted doors of the old town, the cable car to Monte and gardens above the bay.
destinations.html:
Funchal is the capital of the autonomous region of Madeira and a practical base for visitors. The city climbs in terraces from the harbour up a natural amphitheatre of hills, with views over the bay. King Manuel I raised it to city status in 1508, and the name comes from the wild fennel (funcho) the first settlers found growing here.

Start in the centre. The Mercado dos Lavradores, the farmers' market opened in 1940, sells tropical fruit, flowers and the morning's fish, including the black scabbardfish that ends up as espada com banana. A few minutes east, the Zona Velha (old town) is known for the painted doors of Rua de Santa Maria and for its restaurants. Close by stand the Sé cathedral, Blandy's Wine Lodge for Madeira wine, and the CR7 Museum on the waterfront.

What to do

  • Ride the cable car up to Monte, walk the Monte Palace Tropical Garden, then come down on the wicker toboggan.
  • Spend a morning at the Madeira Botanical Garden or the Palheiro Gardens east of the city.
  • Swim at the Lido bathing complex, the Doca do Cavacas rock pools or the pebbles of Praia Formosa.
  • Try a Madeira wine tasting and book a whale and dolphin trip from the marina.

Funchal is also where the island's big events happen: the New Year fireworks over the bay, Christmas lights and the Market Night of 23 December, the Carnival, the Flower Festival and the Wine Festival. Up the hill, the Feast of Our Lady of Monte falls on 15 August.

The south coast is the dry side of the island. IPMA's 1991 to 2020 normals for the Funchal Observatory give about 574 mm of rain a year, almost none of it in July and August, and February afternoons averaging around 20C. The mild winter suits walking and sightseeing. Madeira Airport is about 19 km east, with the municipal tourism office estimating about 17 minutes by car via the VR1 expressway, and the same road takes you west to Câmara de Lobos or east to Caniço in minutes. For the mountains, the road up to Pico do Arieiro starts on the city's edge.

destinations.name: Machico and Caniçal
destinations.tagline: Bay where Madeira's settlers landed, by the Ponta de São Lourenço walk
destinations.summary: Machico is where the Portuguese first landed in 1419: a sheltered sand beach next to the airport, with Caniçal's whale museum and the Ponta de São Lourenço walk beyond.
destinations.html:
Machico lies in a broad bay on Madeira's east coast, just north of the airport. It has a strong place in island history: the regional tourism board records that João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira came ashore here in July 1419 when they reached the island. Today it is a relaxed small town of a seafront promenade, an old church, a marina and a sheltered beach.

The bay has both pebbles and a golden-sand beach, unusual on an island of dark volcanic shores, and the calm water makes Machico beach one of the easier places to swim with children. East along the coast, the former whaling village of Caniçal is home to the Madeira Whale Museum, which tells the story of whaling on the island and of the whales and dolphins that live offshore. Near Caniçal, Prainha is a small natural beach of dark sand.

What to do

  • Swim at Machico beach and walk the seafront to the marina.
  • Learn about whales and whaling at the Madeira Whale Museum in Caniçal.
  • Walk out along Ponta de São Lourenço, the 9 km peninsula at the island's eastern tip.
  • Book a whale and dolphin trip from the east coast.

Ponta de São Lourenço is a partial nature reserve of bare, wind-cut ridges, quite unlike the green interior. As of November 2026 IFCN lists its PR8 trail as open. Visitors book a slot online through SIMplifica and pay unless exempt; check the official status before you go, and carry water and sun protection because there is almost no shade.

Machico is close to Madeira Airport, which makes it a practical first or last night. The VR1 expressway runs past it to Funchal and Caniço, and the tunnel road north reaches Porto da Cruz and Santana on the north coast in a short drive.

destinations.name: Ponta do Sol
destinations.tagline: Small sunny town of banana terraces, a pebble beach and a quiet pace
destinations.summary: Ponta do Sol is a small south-coast town known for sunshine: a pebble beach and pier, banana and sugar cane terraces, and an easy base for the west of the island.
destinations.html:
Ponta do Sol is a small town on Madeira's southwest coast, squeezed into the mouth of a valley between steep cliffs. As its name (Sun Point) suggests, the regional tourism board describes it as generally getting the most hours of sunshine on the island. The centre is a few lanes of old houses, a church and cafes, opening onto a pebble beach and a short pier.

Agriculture shapes the landscape. Banana plantations and sugar cane terraces cover the slopes around the town and down at Madalena do Mar, one of the municipality's three parishes alongside Ponta do Sol itself and Canhas.

What to do

  • Swim from the Ponta do Sol beach and walk out along the pier at sunset.
  • Walk among the banana terraces down to Madalena do Mar.
  • Drive up to the Paul da Serra plateau for the Levada das 25 Fontes walk from Rabaçal.
  • Head west to the sand beach at Calheta or east to Ribeira Brava.

The beach is pebbles and rock; assess the sea conditions before swimming. Facilities include changing rooms, adapted toilets and a bar area. Evenings are quiet and revolve around a handful of restaurants.

Ponta do Sol sits just west of Ribeira Brava, where the VR1 expressway ends, so Funchal and the airport are a straightforward drive and the tunnel road north to São Vicente starts close by. The fast road west continues towards Calheta and Ponta do Pargo, which makes the town a convenient base for walkers heading to the plateau.

destinations.name: Porto Moniz and Seixal
destinations.tagline: Northwest corner of lava rock pools, black sand and laurel forest
destinations.summary: Porto Moniz is famous for seawater pools in volcanic rock; neighbouring Seixal adds a black sand beach, and the Fanal forest and Achadas da Cruz cable car lie close by.
destinations.html:
Porto Moniz sits at the northwest tip of Madeira, where the cliffs drop to a shelf of black volcanic rock. The sea fills natural pools in the lava, continually replenished by seawater, and these pools are the reason most people make the trip. The village behind them is small: a church, a harbour, a few hotels and restaurants serving fish and grilled limpets.

The main Porto Moniz natural pools have been fitted out with a children's pool, changing rooms, a bar, a first-aid post and sunbed hire, while rougher, more natural pools sit nearby. A short drive east along the coast, the parish of Seixal has a small black sand beach at the foot of green cliffs, popular for bodyboarding and kayaking, and its own natural pools by the harbour.

What to do

  • Swim in the volcanic pools at Porto Moniz, ideally on a calm day.
  • Spend a lazy afternoon on the black sand at Seixal beach.
  • Walk among the old laurel trees of the Fanal forest, often wrapped in mist.
  • Ride the Achadas da Cruz cable car down the cliff to the fields and pebble shore below.

The north coast is greener, wetter and cooler than Funchal, and the Atlantic swell here is stronger. The pools and beaches can close or become unsafe in rough seas, so check conditions and follow lifeguard flags. Fanal sits up on the plateau inside the Laurisilva, where fog rolls in quickly; bring a layer even in summer.

Getting here used to mean a long drive on the old cliff road. Today the expressway along the north coast runs through a series of tunnels between Porto Moniz, Seixal and São Vicente, and the tunnel road south links with the VR1 to Funchal, so a day trip from the capital is easy by car. Rockfalls occasionally close sections of the coast road, so check local traffic news after heavy rain.

destinations.name: Porto Santo
destinations.tagline: Neighbouring island with 9 km of golden sand, reached by ferry or plane
destinations.summary: Porto Santo is a separate, smaller island 71 km from Madeira: 9 km of golden sand, calm clear water and a slow pace, reached by the Lobo Marinho ferry or a short flight.
destinations.html:
Porto Santo is the second inhabited island of the archipelago and a different world from Madeira: low, dry and ringed on its south side by one long beach. It lies about 71 km northeast of Madeira, so you cannot drive there. You reach it on the Porto Santo Line ferry, the Lobo Marinho, from Funchal harbour, or by a short flight from Madeira Airport to Porto Santo Airport. Flights also connect it with Lisbon.

The draw is the Porto Santo beach, 9 km of golden sand along the entire south coast, with calm, clear water through the summer. Locals have long valued the sand for what the tourism board calls therapeutic properties. At the western end, Ponta da Calheta looks across to an islet and is a favourite sunset spot.

What to do

  • Spend slow beach days on the 9 km beach and watch the sun go down at Ponta da Calheta.
  • Visit the Casa Colombo museum in Vila Baleira, linked by tradition to Christopher Columbus.
  • Walk the path up Pico do Castelo, which starts at Moledo, for island views. As of November 2026 IFCN lists PS PR2 open; book through SIMplifica and pay the €4.50 standard individual fee unless exempt. Recheck the status on the day.
  • Play the island's 18-hole golf course, or time a visit for the Columbus Festival.

Vila Baleira, the small main town, has the church, the Columbus museum, cafes and the main square. Beyond it the island is mostly open, sandy country with a few hills, so bikes, taxis, hire cars and the island buses cover it easily. Life is quiet out of season, and some businesses close or cut their hours in winter.

Many visitors come for a day trip from Funchal, but the crossing makes a day feel short; one or two nights let you enjoy the beach at an easy pace. Ferry sailing days and times change with the season, and rough seas can cancel crossings, so check the Porto Santo Line timetable before you plan. Our Porto Santo travel guide covers the practical details.

destinations.name: Ribeira Brava
destinations.tagline: South-coast town where the road to the north coast begins
destinations.summary: Ribeira Brava is the hinge between south and north: a seafront town with the Ethnographic Museum, and the start of the fast road through the mountains to São Vicente.
destinations.html:
Ribeira Brava sits at the mouth of a deep valley on the south coast, west of Funchal. It is a compact town of a seafront promenade, a pebble beach, a church square and cafes, and it matters to travellers mostly as a crossroads. The municipal council dates the creation of the municipality to 6 May 1914, making it the youngest in the Madeira archipelago.

The town's main cultural stop is the Madeira Ethnographic Museum, which covers rural island life: farming, fishing, weaving and wine-making. Inland, the valley climbs through the parish of Serra de Água to the Encumeada pass, a viewpoint at 1,007 metres on the island's central ridge, where on clear days you can see both coasts. Encumeada is also a trailhead for several levada walks.

What to do

  • Visit the Madeira Ethnographic Museum and walk the seafront promenade.
  • Drive up the valley to the Encumeada pass for views over both coasts.
  • Take the cable car or a boat down to the pebble beach and farm at Fajã dos Padres, on the coast towards Câmara de Lobos.
  • Continue west to the sunny town of Ponta do Sol for lunch.

Roads explain why Ribeira Brava is so useful. The VR1 expressway runs along the south coast from here through Funchal towards the airport, and the expressway north through the mountains brings São Vicente on the north coast within a short drive, through tunnels that replaced the slow climb over the pass. Before those roads, a trip to the north coast was a long day of hairpins; now it is an easy half-day loop from Funchal.

The flip side is traffic: the junction and tunnel at Ribeira Brava carry much of the island's east-west traffic and can queue at peak times. Most visitors pass through or stop for a meal, but the town also works as a quieter, central base for exploring the west and north.

destinations.name: Santana
destinations.tagline: North-coast base for thatched houses, Pico Ruivo and laurel forest walks
destinations.summary: Santana is the north coast's walking base: thatched triangular houses, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, the path to Pico Ruivo and the Caldeirão Verde levada.
destinations.html:
Santana sits on a green plateau above the northeast coast of Madeira, its fields running to the cliff edge. It is best known for the casas de Santana, small triangular houses with steep thatched roofs and painted fronts, which have become one of the most recognisable images of the island. A group of them is preserved near the town hall as the Santana traditional houses site.

The whole municipality was recognised by UNESCO as a Biosphere Reserve in 2011. It runs up into the highest ground in the archipelago: Pico Ruivo, at 1,862 metres, lies within the municipality, and the forested slopes below hold the Laurisilva. The Queimadas Forest Park is the start of the Levada do Caldeirão Verde (PR9), and at Ribeiro Frio the Balcões viewpoint looks over the central peaks.

What to do

  • See the thatched traditional houses in the town centre.
  • Walk the Caldeirão Verde levada from Queimadas, if the trail is open.
  • Climb Pico Ruivo, or tackle the Pico do Arieiro to Pico Ruivo hike only after IFCN confirms it has reopened; as of November 2026 PR1 is marked closed.
  • Take the short walk to the Balcões viewpoint at Ribeiro Frio.

Mountain walks here are serious undertakings. Classified trails are opened, closed and rerouted after storms and fires, and as of November 2026 visitors must reserve a slot online for IFCN-managed classified trails. The standard fee is €4.50 per trail other than PR1. Madeira residents, children aged 12 or under, and people with a documented disability of at least 60% plus one accompanying legal guardian are exempt from payment; they must still register and book. Read our trail fees guide, check the official trail-status page on the day, and expect cloud, rain and cold at altitude even when Funchal is sunny.

The north coast was once a long, winding drive from the capital. Tunnels and the expressway along the east and north coasts now link Santana with Machico and the airport, so it works as a day trip or as a quiet overnight base for an early start on the trails. Accommodation is mostly small hotels and rural guesthouses.

destinations.name: São Vicente
destinations.tagline: Green north-coast valley town with a chapel built into the rock
destinations.summary: São Vicente is a tidy north-coast town in a green valley, with a chapel carved into a sea rock and easy access to both coasts through the mountain tunnels.
destinations.html:
São Vicente lies where a broad green valley meets the sea on Madeira's north coast. The tourism board describes a population of around 6,000 across three parishes (São Vicente, Ponta Delgada and Boaventura), and forest covers much of its land. The old village centre, a few streets of whitewashed houses with dark stone trim around the parish church, is one of the neatest on the island.

The town's landmark is a small chapel built into a basalt rock at the river mouth, a reminder that the whole island is volcanic. The valley is also known for its lava tubes: the São Vicente caves once offered a guided underground route of around 700 metres, but the regional tourism board lists them as closed (checked November 2026), so do not plan a visit around them.

What to do

  • Walk the old village centre and down to the rock chapel at the seafront.
  • Drive up the valley to the Encumeada pass, where levada walks start on the central ridge.
  • Continue west along the coast to Porto Moniz and Seixal for the natural pools.
  • Head east to the quiet parishes of Ponta Delgada and Boaventura, terraced farmland above the sea.

The north coast is wetter and greener than the south, and weather changes quickly. Bring a rain layer, and if you walk, check the official trail status on the day: classified routes can close after storms and rockfalls, and visitors must book IFCN-managed classified trails in advance (see our trail fees guide).

São Vicente owes much of its accessibility to the tunnel road that crosses the mountains from Ribeira Brava. With it, and the expressway along the north coast, the town is a short drive from the south coast and from Porto Moniz, so it slots easily into a north-coast loop from Funchal. The Fanal forest and the Laurisilva are within reach for a half-day.

beaches.name: Complexo Balnear do Lido
beaches.tagline: Funchal's seafront lido with saltwater pools and ladders into the sea
beaches.summary: A municipal bathing complex built over the sea in Funchal's hotel zone: an adult pool, children's pools, sea access, lifeguards and sun terraces. Open all year.
beaches.html:
The Complexo Balnear do Lido is the easiest place in Funchal to swim when you want a pool, the ocean and a sunbed in the same afternoon. The complex is built out over the rocks on the seafront promenade (Passeio Público Marítimo), in the hotel area west of the centre, and it steps down over several terraces towards the Atlantic. There is a main saltwater pool, shallow children's pools and access points straight into the sea, so you can swim in calm water or go out into the ocean depending on the day.

The municipal company Frente MarFunchal runs it as a paid complex and keeps it open all year. Its list of services includes lifeguards, first aid, changing rooms, lockers, showers, sunbed and parasol hire, Wi-Fi, a bar, a restaurant, a diving centre and a beach shop. The Lido holds a Blue Flag for 2026 and is a named lifeguarded bathing beach for the official season. Access is good for visitors with reduced mobility: the tourism board lists lifts, ramps and amphibious chairs. Sea access depends on conditions; follow on-site instructions.

Tickets and hours (as of November 2026)

  • Entry €6 for adults, €2 for ages 7 to 17, free for children 6 and under accompanied by an adult, with proof of age.
  • Winter hours (25 October to 31 March): daily 09:00 to 18:00.
  • Sunbeds and parasols €2.50 each; combined ticket-and-sunbed deals at the gate.
  • Check the operator's page for summer hours before you go.

The Lido sits on the promenade that leads west to the rock pools of Doca do Cavacas and the free pebbles of Praia Formosa. If you want a beach in the wild rather than a pool by the hotels, the cable-car cove of Praia do Garajau is a short drive east.

beaches.name: Doca do Cavacas
beaches.tagline: Volcanic rock pools on Funchal's west edge, facing Cabo Girão
beaches.summary: A small bathing complex of natural volcanic pools and sun terraces at the west end of Funchal, with sea access, lifeguards and a view of Cabo Girão.
beaches.html:
Doca do Cavacas, once known as Poças do Gomes, is a small bathing complex built around natural pools in black volcanic rock on the western edge of Funchal. Sun terraces sit above the pools, and the view looks west along the cliffs to the headland of Cabo Girão. It is smaller and simpler than the Lido, and the setting is the reason to come.

Frente MarFunchal runs it as a paid complex and lists it as open all year, with lifeguards, first aid, showers and toilets, changing rooms, sunbed and parasol hire, sea access, a support bar and Wi-Fi. For 2026 it is a named lifeguarded bathing beach for the official season (1 June to 15 September). It does not hold a Blue Flag for 2026. Check conditions and on-site instructions before using the pools or sea access. The rock is uneven and slippery near the water, so footwear with grip is worth packing.

Tickets and hours (as of November 2026)

  • Entry €6 for adults, €2 for ages 7 to 17, free for children 6 and under accompanied by an adult, with proof of age.
  • Winter hours (25 October to 31 March): daily 10:00 to 18:00.
  • Sunbeds and parasols €2.50 each.
  • Uneven rock around the pools: not the best choice for small children.

A pedestrian tunnel of about 100 metres links Doca do Cavacas with the free pebble shore of Praia Formosa, so you can combine a pool morning with a beach walk. The fishing harbour of Câmara de Lobos is a short drive further west.

beaches.name: Fajã dos Padres
beaches.tagline: Pebble beach and farm estate at the foot of a 250 m cliff, by cable car or boat
beaches.summary: A pebble beach on a strip of farmland below a 250-metre cliff, reached only by cable car or by boat. Sun terraces, a seaside restaurant and no road access.
beaches.html:
Fajã dos Padres is a fajã, a strip of flat land at the foot of a sea cliff, on the south coast between Funchal and Ribeira Brava. The cliff behind it rises about 250 metres, and there is no road down. You arrive by cable car or by boat, with no road access. Below the cliff are a rounded-pebble beach, a small pier, sun terraces and a working farm that grows tropical fruit and makes wine; the estate says it produces Malvasia Cândida, one of Madeira's rarest grape varieties.

The cable car starts from the Estrada Padre António Dinis Henriques in Quinta Grande and travels about 300 metres along the cliff face in roughly three and a half minutes. According to the estate's own site (as of November 2026) it runs daily from 10:00 to 18:00 for most of the year and until 20:30 between 27 June and 13 September. Children up to 11 ride free and overnight guests ride free; adult tickets are sold through the estate's booking site, and we could not read a current fare there, so check before you go. The estate also allows visitors one hand bag each and requires written authorisation for drones over the property, solarium and beach. Boat access uses the small pier. On the beach there are showers and sunbeds, and the restaurant and bar serve lunch with fish and the estate's produce.

Things to know

  • No road access: cable car from Quinta Grande or by boat.
  • Pebble beach; lifeguard cover is not assured.
  • Restaurant and bar on site; book a table in summer.
  • Check sea conditions before entering the water.

Fajã dos Padres is a good half-day from Funchal or Câmara de Lobos, and pairs well with the glass platform at Cabo Girão, the next headland east. Further west the coast continues to the sheltered pebble bay of Ponta do Sol.

beaches.name: Machico Beach (Praia da Banda d'Além)
beaches.tagline: Golden-sand town beach in Machico Bay, close to the airport
beaches.summary: A golden-sand beach in Machico Bay, built with sand imported from Morocco. Blue Flag in 2026, lifeguards in the summer season and full facilities.
beaches.html:
Machico's town beach, officially Praia da Banda d'Além, is a stretch of soft golden sand at the mouth of the Ribeira de Machico, inside the sheltered bay of Machico on the east coast. The sand is not local: the tourism board says it was imported from Morocco, which is why it looks so different from the grey pebbles of most Madeiran beaches. For anyone who wants a classic sandy beach day on the main island, it is one of very few options.

The bay is protected, the beach is easy to reach from the town centre, and the facilities are complete: changing cabins, showers, toilets, a car park, access walkways and provision for people with reduced mobility. Banda d'Além is a lifeguarded beach in the regional 2026 bathing-water regulations, with a season from 16 June to 27 September, and it holds a Blue Flag for 2026. Cafés and restaurants in the town are a short walk away.

What to expect

  • Imported golden sand in a sheltered bay: rare on Madeira island.
  • Blue Flag for 2026, with lifeguards from 16 June to 27 September.
  • Changing cabins, showers, toilets, parking, access walkways and provision for reduced mobility.
  • Close to Madeira Airport, useful on an arrival or departure day.

From Machico it is a short drive east to the natural sand of Prainha, the Madeira Whale Museum in Caniçal and the coastal walk at Ponta de São Lourenço. For more sandy options, including the long beach on Porto Santo, see our beaches guide.

beaches.name: Ponta da Calheta (Porto Santo)
beaches.tagline: The rocky south-west end of Porto Santo's long beach
beaches.summary: The quieter south-west end of Porto Santo's beach, where the sand meets dark rock and faces Ilhéu de Baixo. Parking, toilets and a restaurant; lifeguard cover is not assured.
beaches.html:
Ponta da Calheta is the south-western tip of Porto Santo, where the island's long beach finally runs out of sand. The tourism board calls the beach here Calheta Beach and singles out its rock formations: dark volcanic outcrops break up the golden sand and run into the water, a change of scene after kilometres of open beach. Across a narrow channel sits Ilhéu da Cal, also known as Ilhéu de Baixo, an islet once mined for lime, and on clear days you can make out the profile of Madeira on the horizon.

This end is quieter and more remote than the stretches near town, but not without services: the tourism board lists a car park, changing rooms, toilets and a restaurant. The regional 2026 bathing-water regulations list the Calheta bathing water with a season of 1 June to 30 September, without assured lifeguard cover, and class it as a limited-use beach. Check local flags and sea conditions before entering; if you are not a confident swimmer, choose a supervised section.

Know before you go

  • Golden sand broken by dark rock, facing Ilhéu de Baixo.
  • Parking, changing rooms, toilets and a restaurant, according to the tourism board.
  • Lifeguard cover is not assured: for supervised swimming, use Fontinha, Cabeço da Ponta or Ribeiro Salgado.
  • Madeira is visible on the horizon in clear weather.

Ponta da Calheta is the far end of Porto Santo Beach, so a long beach walk from the hotel strip ends here. Read the Porto Santo travel guide for getting around the island, or plan the crossing with our Porto Santo day trip page.

beaches.name: Porto Moniz Natural Pools
beaches.tagline: Lava-rock sea pools with lifeguards at Madeira's north-west tip
beaches.summary: Seawater pools shaped by cooled lava on the north-west tip of Madeira, with lifeguards, changing rooms, a bar and a children's pool. Open all year, small entry fee.
beaches.html:
The natural pools at Porto Moniz are a municipal bathing complex built around natural sea pools on Madeira's north coast. Black volcanic rock, formed as lava cooled, encloses a set of pools with a constant inflow of Atlantic seawater. The municipality runs the site as a staffed bathing complex with an entry fee.

That management is what sets these pools apart from wild swimming spots. As of November 2026 the municipality states that lifeguards are on constant duty, and the pools are listed in the regional 2026 bathing-water regulations as a lifeguarded bathing area for a long season, from 15 April to 15 October. There is a separate children's pool, a playground, changing rooms, a bar, a first aid post and sun loungers and parasols for hire. The site holds a Blue Flag for 2026.

Practical details (as of November 2026)

  • Entry: €3 per person over 3 years old, per visit; children aged 3 and under go free. Students and holders of the 65+ card pay €1.50.
  • Hours: open all year, 9am to 5pm in winter and 9am to 7pm in summer, according to the municipality.
  • Check sea conditions and confirm access with the pools before a long drive; year-round opening does not guarantee bathing on the day.
  • Car park and access for people with reduced mobility, according to the tourism board.

Porto Moniz is a natural lunch stop on a north-coast loop. The black-sand Seixal Beach and the Seixal natural pools lie a short drive east, the Achadas da Cruz cable car drops down the cliffs to the south-west, and the misty laurel trees of Fanal are up on the plateau above. For more places to swim, see our guide to Madeira's beaches and pools.

beaches.name: Porto Santo Beach
beaches.tagline: About 9 km of golden calcareous sand along Porto Santo's south coast
beaches.summary: Around 9 km of soft golden sand along Porto Santo's south coast, with calm water, three Blue Flag sections in 2026 and lifeguards in the main bathing zones.
beaches.html:
The beach of Porto Santo is the reason most people make the crossing from Madeira. It runs for around 9 km along the island's south coast, past the town of Vila Baleira towards the rocky point at Ponta da Calheta, and it is everything Madeira island's coast is not: soft, pale golden sand, calm, clear water and space to walk for hours. The regional geology service explains that the sand is mainly calcareous, made from broken shells, corals and calcareous algae, with a few dark grains from volcanic rock.

The sand has a long local reputation for health benefits. An article in the 2011 volume of Anales de Hidrología Médica by geoscientists at the University of Aveiro describes sand baths in Porto Santo's sand being used for about 200 years, "although on a much empirical manner", for rheumatic and orthopaedic conditions, and links any effect to minerals in the warm sand absorbed through the skin. The regional geology service says the sand has been used in sand baths for bone and muscular conditions. Treat it as a local tradition rather than a medical treatment.

Where to swim

  • Three sections hold a Blue Flag for 2026: Fontinha (by Vila Baleira), Cabeço da Ponta and Ribeiro Salgado.
  • The same three are lifeguarded beaches in the regional 2026 regulations: Ribeiro Salgado from 1 May, Fontinha and Cabeço da Ponta from 15 May, all until 31 October.
  • Fontinha, closest to town, has toilets, changing rooms, lockers, sunshades, sun loungers, a first-aid post and food.
  • Services and assured lifeguard cover are concentrated in the designated zones: check local signs and bring water and shade.

Getting here takes either the Lobo Marinho ferry from Funchal or a short flight to Porto Santo Airport; our Porto Santo day trip page compares the two. In town, the Columbus House Museum is a short walk from Fontinha, and the Porto Santo travel guide covers where to stay.

beaches.name: Praia da Calheta
beaches.tagline: Golden-sand beach built with imported sand behind two breakwaters
beaches.summary: Madeira's first man-made beach: golden sand imported from Morocco, calm water behind two breakwaters, free entry, summer lifeguards and a Blue Flag for 2026.
beaches.html:
Praia da Calheta is a beach on Madeira island built with imported sand: opened in 2004 as Madeira's first artificial beach, it was built with yellow sand imported from Morocco and is protected by two sloping breakwaters that keep the water calm. The beach is about 100 metres long, with a large sun terrace of around 7,300 square metres, and sits beside the marina in the village of Calheta on the south-west coast.

Entry is free. The council notes that showers, sunbeds and parasols are paid services (as of November 2026). The tourism board lists sunbed and parasol hire, a bar, changing rooms and first aid, and the breakwaters make the bay popular with families and for kayaking. Calheta holds a Blue Flag for 2026, and the regional government names it a lifeguarded bathing beach for the 2026 season, which ran from 29 June to 30 September. Do not assume lifeguard cover outside those dates. It is a short, man-made beach rather than a wide natural strand. Check space on arrival in summer.

What to expect

  • Imported golden sand, about 100 metres long.
  • Calm water behind two breakwaters; good for children.
  • Free access; sunbeds, parasols, bar and changing rooms.
  • Blue Flag 2026; lifeguards during the summer season.

Another imported-sand beach on Madeira island is at Machico in the east; the natural golden sand is on Porto Santo. Closer by, the pebble bay of Ponta do Sol is a short drive east, and Calheta is a good base for levada walks on the high plateau above the coast.

beaches.name: Praia da Ponta do Sol
beaches.tagline: Small pebble bay in the centre of Ponta do Sol village
beaches.summary: A 160-metre pebble beach in a small bay right in Ponta do Sol village, with summer lifeguards, accessible changing rooms, a bar and parking nearby.
beaches.html:
Praia da Ponta do Sol is the village beach of Ponta do Sol on Madeira's south-west coast: a small bay of rounded pebbles about 160 metres long, set in front of the old village houses and cafés. The cove is sheltered by the cliffs on either side, and the shore is stones rather than sand, so it suits a swim and a sunbathe more than sandcastles.

The tourism board lists changing rooms and toilets adapted for visitors with reduced mobility, a bar, a games area and even a summer library on the beach, with parking nearby. Ponta do Sol is a named lifeguarded bathing beach for the 2026 season (10 June to 14 September); it does not hold a Blue Flag for 2026. As on any Madeira pebble beach, the stones shelve and waves break onto them when there is swell, so check the sea before going in, and wear water shoes if you have them. The village is a short walk from the bay, so it is easy to combine a swim with a coffee or lunch.

Good to know

  • Central and easy to reach on foot from the village.
  • Lifeguards during the official bathing season only.
  • Accessible changing rooms and toilets.
  • Pebble shore: bring water shoes and a thick towel.

Ponta do Sol makes a good stop between Ribeira Brava and Calheta, where the imported golden sand of Praia da Calheta is a short drive west. For a quieter swim with no road at all, try Fajã dos Padres to the east.

beaches.name: Praia do Garajau
beaches.tagline: Pebble cove below the Garajau cliffs, reached by cable car, in a marine reserve
beaches.summary: A sheltered pebble cove at the foot of the Garajau cliffs in Caniço, inside a protected marine reserve. Clear, calm water, a cable car down and summer lifeguards.
beaches.html:
Praia do Garajau is a small pebble beach tucked into a cove at the base of the Garajau cliffs, in the parish of Caniço just east of Funchal. The cliffs shelter it from the north, the shore is rounded stones (calhau rolado), and the water in front lies inside the Garajau partial nature reserve, protected since 1986. Fishing is banned in the reserve and boat traffic is restricted, and the clear water attracts divers.

Most visitors arrive by the Teleférico do Garajau, a cable car opened in 2007 that runs down from the headland by the Cristo Rei statue. As of November 2026, the tourism board lists its hours as 10:00 to 20:00 in summer and 10:00 to 18:00 in winter; we could not find a current official fare, so check at the station. A steep road also winds down the cliff, and Santa Cruz council's January 2021 bathing-water profile describes seasonal restrictions on cars, with pedestrian access retained. Check current signs before driving down. At the bottom there are toilets (including accessible ones), changing rooms, showers, a first-aid post, a restaurant with a terrace and a dive centre. Garajau is a named lifeguarded bathing beach for the 2026 season (15 June to 15 September); it does not hold a Blue Flag for 2026. The tourism board describes calm water in the cove, but check conditions and the beach flags before swimming.

Planning a visit

  • Cable car from the Cristo Rei headland; steep road on foot.
  • Summer lifeguards; check cover on arrival.
  • Snorkelling and diving in a protected marine reserve.
  • Restaurant, showers, toilets and a dive centre at the beach.

Garajau is a popular spot for scuba diving and snorkelling. Pair it with a swim at Funchal's Lido or Praia Formosa, both a short drive west.

beaches.name: Praia Formosa
beaches.tagline: Funchal's long, free pebble beach with a seafront promenade
beaches.summary: About 2 km of grey pebbles on Funchal's western seafront, free to use, with lifeguards in summer, showers, beach bars and a Blue Flag for 2026.
beaches.html:
Praia Formosa is the beach Funchal locals actually use. It runs for about 2 kilometres along the western edge of Funchal, a broad shore of rounded grey and dark pebbles (calhau rolado, as the Madeirans call it) backed by a seafront promenade. Entry is free. In the summer season the shore also has stretches of black sand among the stones, but bring water shoes or a thick towel: most of the beach is pebbles, and they get hot by midday.

The municipal company Frente MarFunchal runs the beach and lists showers, toilets, beach bars, a defibrillator and parking, with sunbeds and parasols for hire (€2.80 each, as of November 2026). Praia Formosa holds a Blue Flag for 2026, and the regional government names it a lifeguarded bathing beach for the 2026 season, which ran from 1 June to 15 September. Do not assume lifeguard cover outside those dates. This is open Atlantic water: check conditions and follow the beach flags before swimming.

Before you go

  • Free access; sunbeds and parasols for hire in season.
  • Lifeguards during the official bathing season; check cover on arrival.
  • Pebble shore: water shoes help.
  • Showers, toilets, beach bars and parking along the front.

At its eastern end a pedestrian tunnel of about 100 metres leads to the volcanic rock pools of Doca do Cavacas, and the promenade continues towards the Lido. To the west the cliffs rise towards Câmara de Lobos and the Cabo Girão skywalk. For an overview of where to swim on the island, see our guide to the best beaches and pools in Madeira.

beaches.name: Prainha do Caniçal
beaches.tagline: A small natural-sand cove near Ponta de São Lourenço
beaches.summary: One of Madeira's few natural sand beaches: a small cove of dark, coppery volcanic sand east of Caniçal. Blue Flag in 2026, lifeguards in summer.
beaches.html:
Prainha, also called Prainha do Caniçal, is a small cove on the dry eastern tip of Madeira, east of the fishing town of Caniçal and on the way to Ponta de São Lourenço. Its sand is natural, which is unusual on this island: the regional geology service describes it as one of the few permanent natural sand beaches on Madeira, fed by old wind-blown dune deposits upstream. The tourism board describes the sand as volcanic and coppery, and the bare, ochre hills around the cove give it a look quite unlike the green north.

The beach is reached on foot from the road above, about 100 metres away, and the geology service rates access as moderate rather than easy. There are parasols and sun loungers, a restaurant, changing rooms and toilets, with a parking area. Prainha is a lifeguarded beach in the regional 2026 bathing-water regulations (season 30 June to 27 September) and holds a Blue Flag for 2026. The same regulations list it as a limited-use beach, so check local signs and respect any restrictions.

Tips for visiting

  • Natural dark, coppery sand: rare on Madeira island.
  • Blue Flag for 2026, lifeguards from 30 June to 27 September.
  • A short walk down from the road; check access arrangements if you have reduced mobility.
  • Restaurant, changing rooms, toilets, sun loungers and parasols.

Prainha fits easily into a day at the eastern tip: walk the trail at Ponta de São Lourenço in the morning, visit the Madeira Whale Museum in Caniçal, then swim here. The golden sand of Machico Beach is a short drive back towards Machico.

beaches.name: Seixal Beach (Praia do Porto do Seixal)
beaches.tagline: A small black-sand beach under green cliffs on the north coast
beaches.summary: A small black-sand beach beside Seixal's harbour, backed by steep green cliffs. Lifeguards in the summer season, showers, a bar and kayak hire.
beaches.html:
Praia do Porto do Seixal is a short strip of black sand next to the small harbour of Seixal, a village on the north coast between São Vicente and Porto Moniz. Sand of any kind is rare on Madeira, where most beaches are pebble or rock, and the dark sand against the steep, green-covered cliffs behind it is the reason people stop here.

The beach sits beside the harbour and the Clube Naval do Seixal, so swimming here feels more sheltered than on the open rocky shore nearby. The tourism board lists showers, a bar and kayak hire, and stand-up paddleboarding and bodyboarding are popular. In the regional 2026 bathing-water regulations Porto do Seixal is a lifeguarded bathing beach, with a season from 1 June to 30 September. Outside that window do not assume lifeguard cover, and the north coast can turn rough quickly, so judge the sea on the day.

Before you go

  • Black sand and clear Atlantic water, with cliffs rising straight behind the beach.
  • Lifeguards during the official bathing season (1 June to 30 September in 2026).
  • Showers, a bar and kayak hire on site.
  • Small and popular in summer: weekdays and mornings are quieter.

Seixal pairs well with the Seixal natural pools a few minutes west and the managed lava pools of Porto Moniz further along the coast. The village is also a gateway to walks in the Laurisilva forest, and São Vicente is the next village to the east.

beaches.summary: Natural rock pools in dark volcanic stone by Laje Beach in Seixal, with toilets, showers and a bar. A small fee; watch for sudden large waves.
beaches.html:
Poças das Lesmas are the natural swimming pools of Seixal, a set of volcanic rock basins on the north coast just west of the village, next to Laje Beach (often called "Jamaica Beach" locally). Dark lava rock encloses pools of clear Atlantic water, and the contrast between the black stone, the turquoise water and the green cliffs behind makes this one of the most striking places to swim on the north coast.

The pools are smaller and less built-up than the complex at Porto Moniz. The tourism board lists toilets, showers and a bar, and an entry fee of €2.50 (as of November 2026). It also warns that large waves can arise suddenly and unpredictably here, so stay alert to the sea and keep away from the most exposed edges, especially when a swell is running. As of November 2026 the tourism board says the pools have had lifeguard supervision since 2024. The separate Laje bathing water is not classified as a supervised beach in the regional 2026 list; this does not establish staffing at Poças das Lesmas on a particular day, so check on arrival.

Good to know

  • Entry fee of €2.50, as listed by the tourism board as of November 2026.
  • Toilets, showers and a bar on site.
  • Sudden large waves are the main hazard: avoid the outer rocks in any swell.
  • As of November 2026, the Clube Naval do Seixal pools, by the harbour, are a free alternative with a bar, terrace and sun loungers.

Combine the pools with the black sand of Seixal Beach a few minutes away, then continue west to Porto Moniz. Our beaches and pools guide compares the island's other bathing spots.
